item.title: Making rivals depend on your system is the secret to America's three centuries of winning
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-ilt-让对手依赖你的体系-是美国赢了三百年的秘密/

item.description: The Dutch, British, and Americans took turns as top dog not by blockading but by getting rivals to stake everything on their maritime system—once they can't live without the shipping lanes and markets, cutting them off becomes the most effective killer short of war.
item.content:encoded:
The Dutch, British, and Americans took turns as top dog not by blockading but by getting rivals to stake everything on their maritime system—once they can't live without the shipping lanes and markets, cutting them off becomes the most effective killer short of war.

Walter Mead breaks down America's three centuries of success into a five-step strategy, then pushes it all the way to China, the Taiwan Strait, and AI deterrence. What you get is a judgment framework you can use for the long term, not news-style opinions.

4:47 Unpredictability is a form of power
‘Unpredictability’ is not madness but a modern power strategy. Mead says post-Cold War US diplomacy relied on ‘letting the whole world know where America's red lines are’ as a pillar of stability, but Trump profits from the opposite: crossing lines, threatening allies, turning commitments into bargaining chips. He saw through a secret of the information age—the marginal cost of lying: the first lie is expensive, the thousandth is nearly free. Clinton, besieged by the Lewinsky scandal, discovered that shame lives only in other people's minds; as long as you keep moving forward, the dogs bark but the caravan passes. Trump scaled that insight to industrial proportions. The cost is borne by the US diplomatic system: when the world's top power itself becomes the unpredictable card, the alliances and rules built on predictability since World War II are rapidly unraveling.

10:00 The final step of global hegemony is cutting off
The Anglo-American maritime order won not through a single battle but a five-step playbook: first, open societies on islands—17th-century Holland tolerated heretics and Jews, and ideas and capital flowed in; then global trade, Dutch merchant ships traversing the world, wealth so abundant that paintings showed Turkish carpets and Brazilian parrots. Third, while continental powers fought over Silesia inland, you grabbed India and Canada globally. The fourth step is the riskiest: instead of imitating Spain's colonial blockades, invite everyone in to do business—the British navy fought pirates, and all merchant ships benefited; Germany and Japan were likewise invited in after the war. The final step is the trump card: once the other side can't live without your grain, rubber, and shipping lanes, cut them off—Germany in World War I suddenly found Argentine grain and Malayan rubber cut off, and its economy collapsed.

16:38 All of China's efforts are about preventing the umbilical cord from being cut
Viewing China through the same framework, you see Beijing knows its own vulnerability well. Mead says, suppose the mainland blockades Taiwan, and the US counter-blockades from a hundred miles off Taiwan's coast: oil can't come in, manufactured goods can't go out, soybean contracts with Brazil and Argentina are voided—China's economy would be strangled. He has discussed these scenarios with officials and scholars at Chinese universities, and this concern has always been present. So China's energy policy should be read in parallel: on one hand, building oil reserves on a scale that surprises outsiders; on the other, ramping up solar and hydro, while mining as much coal as possible. It's not schizophrenia; it's the same thing: pulling out, one by one, the weak points of ‘dependence on the outside world.’ He also warns America not to retreat into isolationism—agriculture and AI both need overseas markets to sustain themselves.

25:50 Each technological dividend needs new institutions to match
Mead starts with the ownership society: at America's founding, the land was full of independent farmers who owned their plots; building a bridge might be good, but it would raise my taxes—that trade-off itself was political education. The railroad era paired with the Homestead Act, as the government gave land to railroad companies and farmers, letting a national market grow. In the 20th century, the suburban single-family home replaced the family farm, paired with tax-exempt municipal bonds and highways, becoming a new wealth distribution machine. Today that machine hits housing prices: young people can't afford to live near work. His remedy is remote work and autonomous driving. If the commuting radius expands from 40 miles to 75 miles, the usable land for housing grows with the square of the radius—the physical space opened by technology can support another two generations. But the prerequisite is institutional ‘infrastructure’—he coined the term info-structure, meaning the institutional and regulatory rules that let AI actually land in hospitals and courts.

40:22 Silicon Valley tilts toward the Tech Hamiltonian camp
American foreign policy debate for centuries has been four rhetorics: Hamiltonians want a strong state to pave the way for capital, Wilsonians want to spread liberal democracy, Jeffersonians fear big government, and Jacksonians are isolationist in peacetime but hit back hard when attacked. The post-Cold War establishment was a marriage of Hamiltonian and Wilsonian, but Trump brought Jefferson and Jackson into the tent. Mead says the truly notable new species is the Tech Hamiltonian. In the 1990s, tech companies liked to say ‘we're a global company, Google has no borders, Washington can't touch us’; AI competition turned tech into a matter of national destiny. Economic stances have shifted too: old multinational car companies wanted borderless labor and markets, while Silicon Valley wants supply chain and IP security, even hoping employees are patriotic—selling code to China is shameful, and colleagues will report you. The commercial core shifting from old multinationals to tech nationalists is the underwater current of America's political realignment.

50:00 The more equipment a great power has, the more it fears technological generational shifts
Mead has been to Ukraine twice. The first time at a drone factory, he saw them converting children's toy trucks into ground drones carrying mines to blow up tanks; a few months later, progress was unimaginably fast. The battlefield is now a gray kill zone, usually with only two or three soldiers operating together, and one of the hardest problems is ‘how to evacuate the wounded’—you need a ground drone with a metal shield to drag people out, accompanied by a swarm of hunter drones to kill the enemy's attack drones. He heard of one wounded soldier who took 63 days to be evacuated from the front line. The changes flip every six months. The irony for America: the great power with the most tanks and aircraft carriers is precisely the one most afraid of this kind of parameter revolution—existing equipment goes from advantage to sunk cost. The Russian Black Sea Fleet has no major battles to fight, yet it's trapped at home by Ukrainian small boats and drones.

54:16 The most important new variable in the Taiwan Strait is Japan
On whether the mainland will attack Taiwan, Mead's judgment: Beijing needs a very high probability of success to cross the threshold—if it fails, it's catastrophic for the initiator. But between ‘attack’ and ‘do nothing’ lies a long gray ladder: for example, requiring all ships bound for Taiwan to first stop at mainland ports for customs clearance, or imposing a soft blockade—actions that change the facts on the ground without triggering an armed US response. The truly new variable on the Taiwan chessboard is not the US attitude but Japan. The Japanese have publicly stated that if China takes Taiwan, Japan's independence is over; they are raising defense budgets, rewriting security doctrines, and reshaping national psychology. Historically, Japan has turned quickly when facing a real threat. How steep Japan's learning curve is, and whether Beijing's calculations must factor in Japan, will be the key to the Taiwan issue in the coming years.

1:10:00 AI actually makes deterrence more credible
Applying Cold War deterrence logic to the algorithmic age, Mead points to a counterintuitive conclusion: deterrence succeeds when the opponent is 100% convinced that ‘if I do X, you will inevitably do Y, and you can and will do it.’ As long as there's a human veto point in the decision chain—‘I might soften at the last moment’—that commitment has a crack. Automating part of diplomatic decision-making and handing it to AI turns retaliation into a mechanism that is executable and won't hesitate—deterrence becomes more credible. But that's the doomsday machine problem from science fiction: decisions of annihilation no longer require humans to bear the consequences. His own assessment of the issue is ‘very interesting and somewhat puzzling,’ and he doesn't think an answer has emerged.

item.title: ECT Isn't What You Think: A Century of Drift from the Back Room to Routine Care
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-08-tpwky-ect-不是你想的那样-从密室到常规治疗的百年漂移/

item.description: Modern ECT is a procedure performed under anesthesia and muscle relaxants, with significant efficacy, but the evidence on memory loss side effects remains incomplete, and societal misunderstanding has led to excessive stigmatization.
item.content:encoded:
Modern ECT is a procedure performed under anesthesia and muscle relaxants, with significant efficacy, but the evidence on memory loss side effects remains incomplete, and societal misunderstanding has led to excessive stigmatization.

If your impression of ECT is stuck on One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, this episode will completely refresh your understanding. Hear about the actual procedure, indications, side effects, and a clinician's perspective.

8:07 The actual ECT procedure
If you or I were to undergo ECT, here's what would happen: first, a risk assessment and informed consent, then a physical exam and fasting overnight. The next morning, at the hospital or outpatient clinic, an IV line and two blood pressure cuffs (on the arm and right leg) are placed, and EKG, EEG, and EMG are connected. The anesthesiologist puts you to sleep, then inflates the leg cuff to restrict blood flow to the right foot, and administers a muscle relaxant (such as succinylcholine). Once the muscles are fully relaxed, a bite block is inserted, and a brief electrical current (lasting a few seconds or even half a second) is delivered through electrodes. The goal is not to make your whole body convulse but to induce a generalized seizure, typically lasting 25-70 seconds. Because the muscles are relaxed, you see almost no external movement—the entire process is visible on the EEG.

14:15 Electrode placement and why right side is chosen
There are several electrode placements: bilateral temporal (like in the movies), bifrontal, and the most common 'right unilateral'—one electrode on the right temple and another on the top right of the head. Right unilateral is used for most people because it has fewer cognitive side effects. Why consider the right side first? Because for about 98% of right-handed people and 70%-90% of left-handed people, language function is in the left temporal lobe. Avoiding left-side stimulation theoretically reduces language-related memory problems. However, right unilateral is slightly less effective than bilateral. During treatment, doctors may switch based on side effects and efficacy: if bilateral causes severe side effects, they switch to right unilateral; if right unilateral is ineffective, they switch to bilateral.

16:20 Seizure threshold and effective dose
The seizure threshold is the minimum amount of current that can induce a seizure. There is no precise measuring device, so doctors estimate a starting dose based on age and then titrate upward from a low dose until a seizure occurs. But treatment is not just about reaching the threshold—the effective dose is usually 2.5 to 5 times the threshold. For bilateral, 2.5 times is sufficient, while right unilateral requires 5 times because unilateral stimulation is less effective at achieving the same result. This dose varies from person to person and must be adjusted through trial and error. If a patient does not have a seizure or the seizure is too short (less than 25 seconds) during a session, the doctor may increase the dose and try again. Treatment is typically three times a week, with a total course of 6 to 18 sessions, or even longer.

20:22 We still don't know exactly how ECT works
Why does giving the brain an electric shock treat depression and catatonia? Frankly, we still don't fully understand. There are several main hypotheses. One is neurotransmitter changes: after ECT, serotonin, dopamine, and GABA (an inhibitory neurotransmitter) all show significant alterations. The increase in GABA itself is anticonvulsant, which may explain why the seizure threshold rises and seizures shorten over consecutive treatments. Second, in the hypothalamus and pituitary, we see large fluctuations in hormones like ACTH, prolactin, and TSH. Third, ECT promotes neurogenesis, with the key molecule being BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor). But how these changes directly relieve symptoms is still not mapped one-to-one. The mechanisms may differ for different diseases (depression, schizophrenia, catatonia), so research continues.

24:24 Depression data: far better than first-line antidepressants
For treating major depression, ECT's key data are quite strong: most studies report remission rates (complete symptom resolution) of 50%-60% and response rates (significant symptom improvement) of 60%-90%. In comparison, the maximum remission rate for SSRI antidepressants is only about 40%. ECT also has a rare benefit—it can reduce the 30-day readmission rate by about half. This is not to say it should be a first-line treatment, nor that it is without risks (relapse or symptom recurrence within 6-12 months is not uncommon); but in patients with treatment-resistant depression and severe suicide risk, these efficacy advantages are hard to ignore.

26:27 Memory issues are the most concerning side effect
ECT's most troublesome side effects center on cognition and memory. Immediately after the procedure, there is confusion lasting from a few dozen seconds to half an hour, and attention and executive function may decline for weeks. Interestingly, most cognitive functions actually improve in the long term—possibly due to improvement in depression. The real problem is memory. Anterograde amnesia (difficulty forming new memories) usually resolves within a few weeks after the course, so many people are restricted from driving or making major decisions during treatment. Retrograde amnesia (loss of past memories) is more concerning to patients: it typically affects memories from the recent months or even years before treatment, and while it often recovers, it can be permanent in some cases. Bilateral treatment is more likely to cause this problem than right unilateral.

34:55 Catatonia: a deadly syndrome often misrecognized
Catatonia is often simplistically classified as a subtype of schizophrenia, but it is actually a psychomotor syndrome that can be triggered by any psychiatric or neurological condition. Patients appear awake, with eyes open, yet are almost completely immobile and mute, and may exhibit stupor, waxy flexibility (arm remains in a posed position without falling). Because they cannot eat or drink and are immobile for long periods, they are prone to malnutrition, pressure ulcers, muscle contractures, and even death. Untreated catatonia has a mortality rate as high as 20%! The most common treatment is benzodiazepines, but ECT is highly effective for catatonia from various causes. The previously mentioned girl with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis (the 'Fire in the Brain' case) developed catatonia; immunotherapy and lorazepam were ineffective, and she eventually recovered with ECT.

48:36 The biggest bottleneck is not efficacy but accessibility
Dr. Lopez believes the biggest obstacle ECT faces today is the difficulty in finding treatment centers. His hospital performs over 6,000 treatments annually across two campuses, averaging about 10-12 sessions per patient. But it is not widespread across the country; many adult and pediatric patients travel from other states for treatment, especially in cases of catatonia due to autoimmune encephalitis in infants, toddlers, and adolescents, where finding an experienced treatment team is extremely difficult. Therefore, improving accessibility is his greatest hope. Additionally, physicians in internal medicine, pediatrics, and intensive care often do not recognize catatonia and are afraid or do not think to consult ECT; thus, 'evangelizing' to non-psychiatric colleagues is also part of his daily work.

item.title: The Supreme Court First Gave Students Constitutional Rights, Then Shrunk Them: From Flag Salutes to Backpack Searches

item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-stuffmissed-美国最高法院先给了学生宪法权利-后来又把搜包和体罚还给校园/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: From refusing to salute the flag to searching backpacks, six rulings gradually map out the constitutional rights of American public school students; the Court, while declaring that "schools are not totalitarian enclaves," also upheld corporal punishment and searches based on reasonable suspicion, narrowing the boundaries of those rights.
item.content:encoded:
From refusing to salute the flag to searching backpacks, six rulings gradually map out the constitutional rights of American public school students; the Court, while declaring that "schools are not totalitarian enclaves," also upheld corporal punishment and searches based on reasonable suspicion, narrowing the boundaries of those rights.

Each ruling is explained in five or six minutes, covering background and key holdings—ideal for listeners who want to grasp the boundaries of speech, corporal punishment, and backpack searches in American public schools in one go.

5:10 The Flag Salute Case: Student Rights Enter the Schoolhouse
Can students really claim First Amendment rights during class? This case actually began with religion: Jehovah's Witnesses families believed saluting the flag violated the commandments against other gods and idolatry, so they refused to salute and pledge. In 1940, the Supreme Court ruled against them, and World War II led more districts to require daily salutes and pledges. West Virginia expelled students who refused to recite the pledge, labeled them delinquents, and parents faced fines or jail. In 1943, the Court reversed 6–3, with Justice Jackson writing on Flag Day: no official can define orthodoxy in politics, nationalism, religion, or other opinions; students need not confess words that contradict their hearts or make empty gestures. This was the first time the Court established that students have some First Amendment rights inside school.

11:21 Official Prayer Ruled Unconstitutional
During the Cold War, America cast itself as a God-fearing nation, adding "under God" to the Pledge in 1954, and more public schools began reading scripture or praying before class. In 1951, New York's Board of Regents asked religious leaders to compose a short, non-denominational prayer, leaving adoption to local districts. Districts that used it allowed students to opt out, but parents of ten students sued anyway. In 1962, Engel v. Vitale struck it down 6–1; the key was not coercion but that the prayer was written by the government, itself constituting an establishment of religion. Justice Black quoted Madison: that the first experiment with our liberties should be a warning; the same power that can establish Christianity to the exclusion of all other religions can easily establish one sect of Christianity. The decision sparked fierce backlash, and the plaintiff families faced ridicule and harassment.

18:31 Armbands Are Constitutional Expression
In December 1965, Des Moines middle and high school students planned to wear black armbands to protest U.S. involvement in Vietnam. The school announced that refusing to remove them would lead to suspension, yet some students—including four siblings—wore them and were suspended. In 1969, the Supreme Court ruled for the students 7–2. The issue was not ordinary dress code but a quiet, passive expression akin to pure speech, and it did not disrupt class. Without evidence of actual or materially substantial interference with schoolwork, schools may not suppress student opinion. The opinion declared that public schools are not totalitarian enclaves; students and teachers do not shed their constitutional rights at the schoolhouse gate. This "substantial disruption" test became the benchmark for campus speech. Justice Black dissented, predicting students would defy nearly all rules, which the hosts called a rather absurd slippery slope.

24:40 School-Sponsored Newspaper Can Be Censored
In 1983, Hazelwood East High School's student newspaper, The Spectrum, had two articles that troubled Principal Reynolds: one on teen pregnancy used pseudonyms but might still identify the interviewee, and a divorce story named and criticized a student's parent. Reynolds decided to delete the entire two pages rather than just the articles, citing lack of time to edit and the need to publish before semester's end. In 1988, the Supreme Court ruled for the school 5–3. The key distinction was between "tolerating student speech" and "promoting student speech": the paper was funded by the school, readers would see it as bearing the school's imprimatur, and the articles were indeed immature journalistically. The Court held that schools may regulate content they sponsor. This drew the first clear boundary around Tinker's rights.

29:46 Corporal Punishment Is Not Cruel and Unusual
Host Tracy suddenly recalled that many teachers kept wooden paddles on their desks when she was young, and research showed corporal punishment has not disappeared in America. In the 1977 case Ingram v. Wright, the school's board was less than two feet long, three to four inches wide, and half an inch thick, with a policy of one to five swats; but Ingram received more than 20 swats in a single incident and needed medical attention. The Court did not dwell on whether the individual case was excessive; it ruled that school corporal punishment does not violate the Constitution. The Eighth Amendment protects convicted persons; prisoners and schoolchildren are separated by "the harsh facts of criminal conviction and incarceration." Schools are open places with teachers and peers as witnesses, and students go home at the end of the day. According to NEA statistics, corporal punishment remains legal in public schools in 17 states and is actually used in 14; boys, Black students, and students with disabilities are paddled at significantly higher rates.

33:52 Backpack Searches Need Only Reasonable Suspicion
In 1980, a 14-year-old New Jersey student, TLO, was reported by a teacher for smoking in the restroom. Vice Principal Choplik searched her purse, found cigarettes and rolling papers, then continued digging and found what appeared to be marijuana and evidence of drug dealing. TLO was convicted and sentenced to a year's probation. In 1985, the Supreme Court upheld the search 6–3. The Court acknowledged that the Fourth Amendment binds school officials and that students have a legitimate expectation of privacy, but it must be balanced against the school's need to maintain a learning environment. Therefore, school searches need not meet the probable cause standard required for police; a lower threshold of reasonable suspicion suffices. The teacher's report gave the vice principal reason to suspect she had cigarettes, and the purse was the obvious place; seeing rolling papers naturally extended suspicion to marijuana, which was also reasonable.

item.title: Criticism That Lands: Lead with High Standards and Trust
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-thinkfast-批评想被听进去-先给高期待与信任/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-thinkfast-批评想被听进去-先给高期待与信任/
item.description: Criticism is accepted not because you soften it with praise, but because the other person sees that the bar is high and you believe they can clear it. In the experiment, a single line — "the standards are high but you can meet them" — tripled the rate at which Black students revised their essays.
item.content:encoded:
Criticism is accepted not because you soften it with praise, but because the other person sees that the bar is high and you believe they can clear it. In the experiment, a single line — "the standards are high but you can meet them" — tripled the rate at which Black students revised their essays.

The originator of stereotype threat research breaks down the mechanism and lands on a replicable experimental script. Twenty minutes of dense information, no generic communication platitudes.

1:04 Identity bias makes people freeze in the moment
When a situation carries a negative label about one of your identities, and the situation matters to you, you worry about being judged by that label. The worry comes from the situation itself; it immediately depresses performance on tests, sports, or intellectual tasks, and over time makes people avoid such situations altogether, shaping who they befriend, where they live, and where they send their kids to school. The anxiety comes not from ability but from the expectation of being defined by a label.

3:10 Social media corners people with labels
Social media's power lies in spreading quick sketches of group images. People have no patience for nuance or exceptions, so it naturally multiplies the situations where you feel you'll be seen through your identity. It occasionally spreads images that reduce threat, but the overall tone is negative. The result: in a diverse society, everyone is more vigilant about their identity and what others might think.

6:16 A 15-minute self-reflection can raise grades
In racially integrated classrooms, Black students constantly worry about being underestimated. Teachers asked seventh graders to spend 15 minutes writing a short essay about the people and things they value most. White students were barely affected, but Black students used the opportunity to signal to the teacher that "I am more than that label." Their grades began to rise, entering a positive feedback loop: better grades → less vigilance about the label → even better grades. The intervention costs almost nothing, yet it changes long-term trajectories.

9:20 In diverse settings, the vigilance: remember or forget
The author calls this state churn. When people from different identity backgrounds work together and the stakes are high, you oscillate between two choices: remember that others may interpret you through your group's stereotype to protect yourself, or forget it and relax into trusting the people in front of you. This is not fragility; it is real situational pressure. When the stakes are high, it constantly drains attention that should go to the task.

12:24 High standards plus trust make feedback stick
In the experiment, students wrote an essay about their favorite teacher and received critical feedback. Two delivery methods — direct feedback, or feedback preceded by a "positive high hat" — were trusted by white students but highly distrusted by Black students. A third method added just one line: "We have high standards because the essay will be published; I've read your essay and I believe you can meet them." Under this condition, Black students took the essay home to revise at three times the rate of the other conditions.

14:26 Never assume others already trust you
Having served as dean and provost for years, Claude believes the most useful ability is recognizing that every person you work with needs that signal of respect. Society's common mistake is assuming trust already exists, but in reality, people worry about how you view the group they belong to. Truly effective leaders excel at sending this signal first: even if employees disagree with a decision, if they feel respected as individuals and for their potential, the team atmosphere changes completely.

17:35 Let people see you as human before trust
Claude breaks good communication into three parts. First, let the other person know you understand what the situation means to them; when power is unequal, the higher-status person must release a safety signal. Second, near-paranoid clarity — beating around the bush destroys valuable information. Third, warmth and goodwill — people need to confirm that the person across from them is a good person before they hand over trust. Matt sums it up as connection, clarity, and care.

item.title: Latin Won't Train a Surgeon: Make Exams Hard, Not Just Useless
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-econtalk-拉丁文练不出外科医生-考试难-不如考得有用/

item.description: Latin won't train a surgeon: skills barely transfer. If you believe 'the harder, the better for the brain,' a nation's brightest will be wasted on the most useless knowledge—that's the lesson of the Qing dynasty civil exams.
item.content:encoded:
Latin won't train a surgeon: skills barely transfer. If you believe 'the harder, the better for the brain,' a nation's brightest will be wasted on the most useless knowledge—that's the lesson of the Qing dynasty civil exams.

Putting imperial civil exams, military selection, and modern transfer experiments on the same chain of evidence is a rare move that bridges history and talent assessment, and the two sides genuinely clash.

10:03 Wrong exam content dooms even smart candidates
Hong Xiuquan failed the Qing imperial exams at least four times. After his last failure, on the road home, he had visions and came to believe he was the younger brother of Christ, eventually launching the Taiping Rebellion—which Daisy calls possibly the deadliest civil war in human history, with deaths around 30 million. The losers weren't just Hong: exam slots were far fewer than the candidate pool, and many kept trying into their forties and fifties, with teaching as their only fallback. Daisy adds that the deeper cost fell on those who passed: they mastered the eight-legged essay but knew nothing of the science and mathematics transforming the world. When the brightest young minds can only practice rigid formats, the nation bleeds in two directions at once.

22:51 British civil service reform was elite self-replication
The Northcote-Trevelyan Report is often seen as the founding document of the modern British civil service, but Daisy supports the revisionist view: under the banner of a unified exam, it pushed Oxford and Cambridge classics graduates into key posts. Benjamin Jowett, Master of Balliol, worked behind the scenes to place his classics students throughout the empire. Michael Coolican's 'No Tradesmen and No Women' argues that the 1854 report reduced the most blatant buying and selling of offices but also snuffed out the professional exams that departments had been developing. Exams aren't inherently bad at selecting people; what matters is what they test—whether they select for merit or for people like yourself.

35:58 Bureaucracies without price signals correct via corpses
Daisy attributes bureaucratic failure to a lack of feedback: no price mechanism, no profit and loss, so departments can't know if their policies save or harm. The military seems a counterexample, but military bureaucracies err constantly in peacetime; Britain, after nearly every long peace, stumbled into crisis in the first year of war, as with the shell crisis of WWI. What forces correction isn't internal inspection but mass death on the battlefield. She calls this a more brutal correction mechanism than prices. To make bureaucracies reliable, you first need a signal that reveals consequences; otherwise, no matter how rigorous the exam, it can't save the quality of everyday decisions.

43:06 Royal Navy won by testing navigation, not Latin
Daisy reminds us that in Victorian times, Britain's true pillar was the Royal Navy, not the army. As early as 1677, after successive defeats by the Dutch, Samuel Pepys introduced an oral exam for lieutenants: three senior officers grilled candidates on how to command a ship. Over the next century, navigation, charting, and trigonometry entered written exams, and chart-makers like Nelson, Cook, Flinders, and Bligh all passed through this gate. Daisy uses this to contrast two exam traditions: Pepys tested skills needed immediately; Macaulay and Northcote-Trevelyan later wanted classical languages. One served navigational safety, the other served class distinction—so the outcomes naturally differed.

47:31 Content irrelevant? Macaulay's screening theory misses a key link
Here's the highlight: Daisy reads aloud Macaulay's 1833 parliamentary speech. In essence, whatever a generation teaches, the top performers will inevitably be the smartest, most diligent, and most ambitious youth; so Cambridge could teach Ptolemy instead of Newton and still produce excellent students; teaching Cherokee instead of Greek would still make the Cherokee experts standouts; even astrology and alchemy would do. Another MP praised it as the most practical speech in parliamentary history, but Daisy bluntly says it's more like being carried away by his own rhetoric, completely missing that 'what you learn really matters.'

51:21 Dead branches and corn: wrong content makes discipline wasted water
Daisy uses Abraham Flexner's 1917 rebuttal to close out Macaulay. Flexner said proponents of mental discipline are like Egyptian priests: they plant a row of dead branches and then water them on schedule for discipline's sake. If you plant corn, you get the same discipline plus a harvest. In contrast, American medical schools forced aspiring doctors to study Greek and Latin before touching medicine; Flexner's answer: medicine itself is hard enough, and using it to train the mind is far more efficient than using dead languages. Daisy agrees: spending the best years of the most talented on discredited or useless knowledge only benefits rivals who teach their youth real knowledge.

59:21 Rectangles don't train triangles: transfer needs identical elements
Thorndike designed a cleaner controlled experiment: people practiced estimating rectangle areas until they improved markedly, then tested on triangle areas—transfer was nearly zero. If even such similar tasks don't transfer, the claim that classical languages sharpen the mind is even less credible. Thorndike's explanation was identical elements: transfer occurs only when old and new tasks share components; far transfer is largely broken. Daisy derives a design principle: to select navigators, test navigation and trigonometry; to select doctors, test medicine. Effective exams connect difficulty directly to real tasks.

item.title: Global Liquidity Peaks: The More Aggressively You Spent on AI in H1, the Sooner You Get Discounted
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-cn38ff4a-全球流动性见顶-上半年越激进砸-ai-的公司-越先被折价/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-cn38ff4a-全球流动性见顶-上半年越激进砸-ai-的公司-越先被折价/
item.description: A stock market rally needs new money to keep buying. Global liquidity is already showing signs of peaking, and the companies that most aggressively invested in AI in the first half are shifting from being rewarded to being discounted.
item.content:encoded:
A stock market rally needs new money to keep buying. Global liquidity is already showing signs of peaking, and the companies that most aggressively invested in AI in the first half are shifting from being rewarded to being discounted.

This episode ties US AI capex, Hong Kong IPO demand, and household balance sheets into a single capital chain, offering a macro framework that doesn't treat AI as a cure-all.

0:33 Low IPO break rate is not a good sign
Don't take the low break rate of Hong Kong IPOs as a sign of market strength. In the first half of this year, the break rate was only around 10-20%, far below the normal level of roughly half-and-half under a market-driven mechanism. That means the participants were mostly short-term speculative arbitrage funds, not long-term investors. Recently, the supply of new listings has decreased, and some IPO-related funds have had problems, but the two newly listed companies still broke their issue price, showing that temporary supply-side controls haven't solved the fundamental issue: Hong Kong also faces peaking liquidity.

12:07 The more aggressive the AI spending, the sooner the punishment
Market sentiment reversed within a quarter. Before Q1, the capital market rewarded aggression: the louder the AI capex talk, the higher the valuation. But by the end of July, when half-year reports were released, any internet giant that had made aggressive capital expenditures in H1—especially those that burned through free cash flow—got discounted, and even Google was not exempt. Q2 was the most FOMO quarter across the entire supply chain; everyone rushed to spend before prices rose, and inventory still supported gross margins. By Q3, inventory is depleted, the impact of price increases returns, and the negative factors will appear together.

15:54 Nvidia is closer to Cisco in 2000
Nvidia's earnings look good, but its cash flow is changing. Before the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, Cisco introduced 'rent-to-own' to help customers finance purchases, recognizing future revenue as sales upfront. Nvidia is now also pushing rent-to-own. In its latest report, free cash flow fell by half quarter-over-quarter, and accounts receivable are far above historical levels—which some speculate may be partly related to the credit enhancement and payment structure from rent-to-own. So Nvidia may have reached a point where it needs more aggressive financial tactics to sustain market expectations, similar to Cisco's situation back then.

33:21 Primary market money comes from bullets fired three years ago
The answer lies in the timing of fund raises. The money concentrated in AI and robotics from H2 2025 to H1 2026 mainly comes from funds raised at the market peak in 2020-2022. From 2023 to 2025, they barely invested, until they saw state capital placing bets when no one dared and making the most money—the stories of CXMT and YMTC, two large language models, and two major chip companies stimulated market-based funds. The mindset became: copy the state's playbook. So this is not a rational long-term increment, but more like a delayed emotional release.

47:31 New property policy removes households from the financing chain
The recent property policy is not about rescuing developers but about dismantling the old financing loop that put households in it. In the past, buying off-plan housing meant households played the role of financing objects in the investment-driven chain: paying first, receiving the apartment later. The policy pushes the chain toward marketization, so buyers now get completed homes and only act as consumers, shifting risk back to developers and financing institutions. The policy was introduced when housing prices were near the bottom, aiming to stabilize the denominator of the asset side first and avoid panic during a decline. Japan after the 1990s and China's coal and mining industry consolidation followed similar paths.

1:01:34 A slow bull is not a slogan but a chip structure
A slow bull doesn't come from shouting; it comes from layering market chips by duration: at the bottom are low-valuation, high-dividend blue chips held by insurers as long-term money that rarely trades; above that are public funds and index funds, functioning close to a market stabilization role; CSFC and Huijin sit at a higher level to adjust the index; and at the top are retail investors, private funds, and active management money. New insurance regulations require liabilities and assets to match in duration, yield, and liquidity, institutionally ensuring that long money invests long, medium money invests medium, and short money invests short—not allowing short-term household money to be put into ten-year illiquid assets.

1:22:49 Crises grow bigger with each bailout; at least one and a half bubbles
Since the dollar left gold in 1971, global central banks have become increasingly accustomed to directly intervening in crises with money printing, acting faster each time. The quantitative easing after 2008 was supposed to be cleared during the rate hike cycle, but it was interrupted by political intervention, and then COVID hit in 2020, so an even larger wave of money printing was added before the previous bubble had dissipated—today we have accumulated at least one and a half bubbles. Central bank governors have learned to print even more money at the first sign of crisis, and the endogenous result is that inflation, financial asset appreciation, and wealth inequality all intensify simultaneously. As long as bubbles are not allowed to clear, the world may face some form of prolonged stagflation.

item.title: Central Banks Won't Kill the $100 Bill: It's a $2.5 Trillion Interest-Free Loan
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-oddlots-央行不愿废除百元美钞-那是一笔-2-5-万亿无息贷款/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-oddlots-央行不愿废除百元美钞-那是一笔-2-5-万亿无息贷款/
item.description: Cash use is declining, yet the dollar in circulation hits new highs. Central banks have an incentive to keep printing $100 bills: this money is effectively a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the U.S. government, at the cost of enabling global money launderers.
item.content:encoded:
Cash use is declining, yet the dollar in circulation hits new highs. Central banks have an incentive to keep printing $100 bills: this money is effectively a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the U.S. government, at the cost of enabling global money launderers.

This episode breaks down money laundering from 'bank wire transfers' into watches, tractors, casino chips, and VAT loopholes, and explains why central banks are reluctant to abolish the $100 bill.

5:09 Money laundering scale hasn't changed in thirty years
The most commonly cited estimate for money laundering is 2% to 5% of global GDP annually, which at today's roughly $100 trillion GDP means $2 trillion to $5 trillion. This figure comes from a rough estimate by former IMF chief Michel Camdessus in the late 1990s, and no one has since provided a better answer. Oliver warns that what should be more alarming is that this percentage hasn't changed in thirty years: decades of anti-money laundering efforts haven't shrunk the criminal economy, only barely kept it from growing faster than the overall economy.

9:10 Banks spend $200 billion a year on AML with near-zero effect
Banks complaining about KYC costs isn't just whining. The 1970 Bank Secrecy Act in the U.S. and the 1989 FATF global norms forced banks to hire compliance teams and install AI monitoring software. LexisNexis estimates global AML compliance costs about $200 billion a year—enough to end world hunger and provide clean water to everyone. But the system generates massive numbers of suspicious activity reports, and launderers still stay ahead of regulators. The problem isn't that banks aren't trying; it's that the whole system is costly, has weak feedback, and almost no one is held accountable for results.

12:14 Trade-based laundering is an order of magnitude bigger than cash smuggling
Cash smuggling makes laundering within the banking system look small, but the bigger chunk doesn't involve money at all: value is hidden in goods. Mexico receives about $25 billion in cash annually, while U.S. exports of John Deere and Caterpillar equipment become the counterpart for drug cartels; European luxury goods flow to China, and from China drugs and goods are imported, with triangular trade settled through misinvoicing. Global Financial Integrity estimates trade-based laundering at about $1 trillion a year. A million-dollar watch worn through customs is far easier than moving a million in cash.

17:18 The Vancouver model: Chinese cash demand meets drug cash supply
China caps each person's annual foreign exchange at $50,000, yet wealthy Chinese have large spending needs abroad. The Vancouver model matches this demand with the dollar cash supply of drug cartels: cash bags are handed to Chinese gamblers outside Canadian casinos, the money is lost at the tables, and the gamblers owe a debt. That debt is offset by renminbi transactions on the Chinese side and subsequent drug sales. Viewed alone, the gambling looks like a loss; across the whole chain, it's a triangular settlement that simultaneously repatriates drug money and moves Chinese capital out. The model later expanded globally, with luxury goods, daily necessities, and drugs as vehicles for moving value.

23:25 VAT loopholes let the same goods repeatedly extract 20%
The EU's zero-rated cross-border transactions were meant to avoid tax authorities checking each other, but they became an ATM: goods entering the UK from Ireland don't incur VAT, and when sold to a related shell company, 20% is added; that shell exports the goods back to Ireland and claims a refund from the UK tax authority for the 20% never paid. This circular movement is why it's called carousel fraud. The UK largely suppressed it with multi-agency crackdowns, but fraudsters moved to the continent, where it now amounts to about €50 billion a year, spreading from Lithuania to Portugal. Criminal organizations have no upper limit on competition: the more they cooperate, the bigger they get.

27:27 No one uses cash, yet central banks print record amounts
In the digital payment era, cash transactions are only about 9% in the UK and 13% in the US, so paper currency supply should logically shrink. After Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey articulated the banknote paradox in 2009, the phenomenon intensified: UK currency in circulation doubled, and the US approached $2.5 trillion. Central banks' explanation of 'store of value' doesn't hold—surveys show the average American adult has only about $400 on hand, while per capita currency in circulation exceeds $7,000. The Fed estimates about 65% of US banknotes are abroad, but that just pushes the problem across borders: no one knows who actually holds these notes.

32:31 The $100 bill is a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the government
Seigniorage isn't simply profit from printing money: a $100 bill costs 9 cents to produce, but it isn't 'sold' to you—you can redeem it for goods at face value anytime, so public cash holdings are essentially an interest-free loan. With nearly $2.5 trillion in circulation, the US government gets interest-free funds equivalent to about 6% of its debt; federal interest payments are about 19% of the budget, and if that $2.5 trillion had to pay interest, it would add about another percentage point. That's why central banks don't want to hear about abolishing the bill.

47:51 AML incentives are inverted: more reports, less crime prosecuted
Suspicious activity reports were meant to be real-time intelligence for law enforcement, but reality is the opposite: banks hire thousands of compliance officers to file reports, law enforcement lacks resources to read them, and most reports go into a black hole; banks can be fined billions for missing a report, but get no reward for doing it right. Side effects include debanking—many suspected individuals, including many Muslims, get cut off from financial institutions. The guests' solution isn't hiring more compliance officers but generating fewer reports, reading them seriously, and actually prosecuting financial criminals, raising the cost of laundering rather than drowning everyone in paperwork.

item.title: Russia Is Stuck in Ukraine but Still Has the Strength to Open a New Front Against NATO
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-hiddenforces-俄罗斯陷在乌克兰-仍有余力对北约开新战线/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-hiddenforces-俄罗斯陷在乌克兰-仍有余力对北约开新战线/
item.description: Russian forces have not won in Ukraine, but the war of attrition has produced the world's most advanced drone-infantry combat experience. The guest argues Russia is fully capable of launching a limited probe against NATO, and the window is in the final stretch of Trump's term.
item.content:encoded:
Russian forces have not won in Ukraine, but the war of attrition has produced the world's most advanced drone-infantry combat experience. The guest argues Russia is fully capable of launching a limited probe against NATO, and the window is in the final stretch of Trump's term.

The guest is the Wall Street Journal's chief foreign correspondent, who was in Kyiv on the day of the 2022 invasion. His assessment of Russian capabilities and European fractures is far more concrete than what TV commentators offer.

19:16 Trump's abandonment rhetoric may be taken seriously by Putin
Everyone is speculating whether John Ratcliffe's secret visit to Russia was about negotiating terms. The guest's judgment is that the visit was more about delivering a message on Trump's behalf: don't take the TV talk about "America not caring about Europe" literally—if Russia invades Lithuania, Estonia, or Finland, the U.S. will send troops. The reasoning is that Moscow, bogged down in Ukraine, urgently needs to cut European support for Kyiv, and escalating to probe NATO is one option. Trump's earlier remarks like "Europe is a bunch of freeloaders" give Putin room for misreading, so a dedicated trip to clarify the red lines makes sense. To be clear: the guest has no intelligence from inside that room; he is explaining why this account is "perfectly plausible," not confirming it.

21:27 The Russian military is not exhausted and can still open a limited front
Is Russia, having failed to take Ukraine by force, unable to open another front? The guest's answer is blunt: it absolutely can fight a "limited front"—not tanks rolling across Poland to Paris, but making trouble in the Baltic direction, such as sealing the Suwalki Gap, that narrow land corridor. He says the Russian and Ukrainian armies are the only two in the world that have turned modern drone-infantry combat into a daily routine. Stories of a 20-person Ukrainian drone squad destroying an entire traditional battalion are widely told, but the Russian side has the same technology: 20 Russians could likewise wipe out a NATO battalion that hasn't trained against drones. The outside world thinks Russia is getting weaker, but it overlooks that Russia is also the side being tempered in this technological revolution.

22:31 NATO might not even have Poland rescue Lithuania
A war game simulating a Russian invasion of Lithuania led the guest to a deeply unsettling conclusion: even Poland did not send troops to save Lithuania, let alone other allies. The reason is not insufficient military strength but that Russian forces advance too quickly, and with nuclear deterrence hanging over, allies would hesitate over "whether to enter," creating a chain of inaction. The guest says Moscow has factored this into its options. He also cautions that this is different from before 2022—then, one could clearly see over a hundred thousand Russian troops massing on the German-Belarusian border; now there is no such physical preparation. So the most direct escalation may not be a conventional invasion but rather small, ambiguous, deniable attacks (first hitting warehouses or drones).

23:40 Russia is probing NATO's limits with drones
In the current phase, with no signs of a massed army, Russia still holds a set of low-cost, low-attribution options: a limited strike on a NATO warehouse near Poland or Romania, or using captured and modified Ukrainian drones to create an incident, then watching whether NATO splits and whether the U.S. steps in. The guest points out that such probing is already underway—an armed drone struck a Ukrainian aircraft parked at Leipzig Airport in Germany, and only a drone malfunction prevented casualties. Russian risk-taking is steadily rising, and the West has yet to give a serious response. The senior European officers he has spoken with all believe the most dangerous window is the next one to two years, roughly in the final stretch of Trump's term—the Kremlin will want to act before the U.S. might let go.

27:53 Putin wants Ukraine disarmed, not a ceasefire
Would Putin accept a decent ceasefire agreement? The guest's view is that just looking at what is on the negotiating table makes it clear: Russia's demands have always included not just territory but also capping the size of Ukraine's military, restricting weapons types, and cutting off Western military aid. In his words, Russia wants to make Ukraine "lose its ability to defend itself"; not neutrality but "castration," so it cannot resist again in the next phase of war—a year, five years, or ten years later. Putin signed Minsk-1 and Minsk-2 and violated both. So the guest quotes a former Ukrainian foreign minister's summary: this war will end in only one of two outcomes—the end of Ukraine, or the end of the Russian imperial project. Waiting for the other side to have a change of heart is not an option.

31:08 Street protests can decide the fate of a wartime cabinet
Kyiv's recent personnel earthquake looks on the surface like an anti-corruption purge, but the key mechanism lies elsewhere: with elections frozen during wartime, the president's legitimacy rests on the ballast of "street support." Zelensky initially fired Defense Minister Fedorov, who championed drone innovation, because he needed the support of Commander-in-Chief Syrskyi. After Fedorov was dismissed, Kyiv's elite took to the streets in protest—small but enough to make the president reverse course: he removed Syrskyi, replaced him with a younger general more popular at the front, and appointed a defense minister with an intelligence background acceptable to all sides. Ukraine's independent anti-corruption agency can still investigate people in the president's inner circle. Zelensky once tried to change the law to bring the agency under his control, but within a week he backed down under street pressure. When elections are absent, the square becomes the election.

38:37 Resistance comes from memory, not heroism
To sum up Ukrainians' persistence as patriotic heroism misses what truly drives them. The guest says that when Russian forces take a Ukrainian town, one of the first things they often do is use bulldozers to demolish monuments to the victims of the 1930s Holodomor famine—they want to delete a memory. Russian state television talks about how to "re-educate" Ukrainians, making them forget their language and culture and become Russians. Around World War II, the Soviet Union carried out systematic purges of Ukraine's cultural elite. The guest, in his childhood, had no idea those writers existed because the collective memory had been erased. Today's Ukrainians are almost all descendants of survivors of that meat-grinder history, carrying trauma in their bodies. It is the fear of "never again" that makes them prefer to die on the battlefield than return to those days.

45:59 Half a million veterans held the first wave of collapse
On the night of February 23, 2022, most Kyivites still did not believe there would be war. The guest remembers that his experience in Kabul and Baghdad taught him that "impossible" can flip overnight, but ordinary Ukrainians had no such reference. What kept the country from collapsing in the first days was the eight-year war in Donbas: that fighting was far from Kyiv, but it trained roughly 500,000 Ukrainians who had fought against Russian forces, and volunteer organizations evolved into a flexible, daring force. The psychological threshold had already been crossed in Donbas—"we know what they look like, we know how to fight." Because of that experience, Putin's expected quick collapse did not happen, and the West's expectations were also broadly wrong.

item.title: Why Your Preschooler's Hitting, Biting, or Kicking Is a Bid for Bodily Autonomy
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-parentmojo-孩子打咬踢不是坏行为-是在夺回身体自主权/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-parentmojo-孩子打咬踢不是坏行为-是在夺回身体自主权/
item.description: Stop asking how to make the hitting stop. For a three- or four-year-old, hitting, biting, and kicking are often the only tools left to say "I have no say" when adults control nearly every aspect of their body. Give back a little choice, and the behavior eases.
item.content:encoded:
Stop asking how to make the hitting stop. For a three- or four-year-old, hitting, biting, and kicking are often the only tools left to say "I have no say" when adults control nearly every aspect of their body. Give back a little choice, and the behavior eases.

Most approaches repeat "no hitting" and add punishment, without touching the need behind the behavior. This episode treats aggression as a need signal, and models scripts and cases for negotiating with teachers.

4:21 Hitting is a child's cry that their body isn't their own
Preschool is often the first place where a child's body is controlled by an adult other than their parents for nearly every arrangement: where to sit, how to sit, when to speak, when to move. In the prior three years, they could largely decide when to run and when to go to the bathroom. Sitting on the carpet for 20 minutes without moving is a real deprivation of autonomy; and a three- or four-year-old lacks the language to assert "my body, my say," so hitting and kicking become one of the few tools left. So when you get that call from the teacher, don't rush to lecture about "hands to yourself." Ask instead: how much say did this child have over their own life before this, and what can we give back?

6:42 Kindergarten readiness is really compliance training
Teachers often say that a high proportion of children at a certain preschool are kindergarten-ready, but the core definition of that readiness is execution: when the teacher says sit, you sit, even if you're mid-task, even if your body is overloaded. Parents worry that if a child doesn't comply now, they won't get into a good elementary school, a good college, a good life. But the price a child pays for this definition is learning to suppress the feeling of "what I need right now." Teachers aren't villains either; they themselves need competence, child safety, ease, and even the satisfaction of power. Many entered education to repair their own childhood wounds, yet only know power-over relationships. Seeing both sides' positions opens room for negotiation.

9:24 We accommodate ourselves but refuse to accommodate children
If adults feel overloaded at a party, we arrive early, leave early, retreat to a quiet room, or wear noise-canceling earplugs—we find this natural. But when it comes to children, beyond routine things like extended test time, we immediately worry that "too much accommodation will spoil him, and he won't survive in the real world." The truth is that adults grant themselves far more accommodation than they allow children. The original piece offers a vivid image: a bigger, stronger adult picks you up without explanation and carries you from a quiet room back to the middle of a noisy party—if that happened to an adult, you'd immediately see it as a violation of bodily autonomy; when it happens to a child, we look away.

12:11 The fix lies before the behavior, not in the behavior itself
Repeating "no hitting" doesn't work because that's not the knowledge the child lacks. You need a different set of questions: What happened in the seconds before the bite? What else happened earlier that day? Is there a move or a new baby in the child's life? A sensory-overloaded child who loses control when pushed in line might do better at the front, back, or outside the line; a child who struggles with transitions needs a few minutes' warning. Analogy: when your partner snaps at you at night over nothing, it's usually not about the words in that moment but about an earlier argument, lack of sleep, and a cascade of stress. If the other person then says "your attitude needs work," you'd explode too; yet we often do only the latter to children.

15:10 Talking to the teacher: don't blame, listen to the 'no'
Telling the teacher "please change your approach" will almost certainly hit a wall. A safer opening is to set aside judgment and reconstruct the facts: not who's to blame, just what actually happened; and include family changes, which are context the teacher can't see. Once you've figured out whether the trigger is sensory or about autonomy, then empathize with the three things behind the teacher's behavior: competence, child safety, and the need for a breather. The request must land on a concrete, executable change, like "Can the child sit on a ball outside the circle?" If the teacher refuses, the key isn't the refusal but the 'no'—what need is the teacher still protecting? Find a way that meets both needs.

16:07 A nap-time conflict resolved cleanly
Jen's daughter Carys, at age three, couldn't nap. The teacher required her to lie down; she was bored and frustrated—her need was to play. The teacher had two needs: state regulations required offering a nap, and nap time was also the teacher's break. The solution they found was to move her mat to a slightly separate corner, where she could play quietly with soft toys that didn't roll, while the teacher could see her through the window from the break room. The child kept her right to free play, the teacher kept the rule and the break, and Jen escaped the dilemma of tattletale calls. This example shows that "negotiating by need" isn't empty talk: everyone gives a little, but everyone's core need is preserved.

17:53 All methods boil down to one question
Compress all the above into one sentence: stop asking "how do I make the hitting stop" and ask instead "what need is this behavior communicating?" Hitting, biting, and kicking are surface signals; the real message might be "I need sensory relief" or "I need some say over my body." Once the need is correctly named, a path to meet it can be designed; and it's almost always the adult who changes the environment, because changing how the adult shows up is far easier than changing the child.

item.title: Thailand Floods Wreck the Hard Drive Industry: The Biggest Falls, the Runner-Up Takes the Crown
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-asianometry-泰国洪水重创硬盘业-最大的厂跌倒-老二捡了王座/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-asianometry-泰国洪水重创硬盘业-最大的厂跌倒-老二捡了王座/
item.description: A Thai flood reshuffled the hard drive hierarchy: Western Digital's shipments fell 51% quarter-over-quarter, while Seagate only dropped 8% and overtook to take the top spot.
item.content:encoded:
A Thai flood reshuffled the hard drive hierarchy: Western Digital's shipments fell 51% quarter-over-quarter, while Seagate only dropped 8% and overtook to take the top spot.

This flood offers a complete case study of the risks of geographically concentrated manufacturing supply chains—industrial estate siting, zero inventory, and single-point bottlenecks all detonate at once.

6:13 Flood dikes gave hard drive factories a false sense of security
The industrial estates sit on a floodplain north of Bangkok, converted from rice paddies. To guard against floods, developers built ring dikes up to two meters high, secondary wave walls, pumps, and drainage systems; the estates quickly grew into small cities with housing and shops. But this engineering may have misled everyone. When the real flood season hit in 2011, seven industrial estates were inundated within two weeks. Research later suspected that such seemingly complete infrastructure created a false confidence—the belief that even heavy rain would be safe. In other words, what manufacturers bought was not safety but an illusion of risk management.

8:24 Reservoir releases were not the culprit; local rainfall was
After the disaster, dam operators were blamed for releasing water too late, with criticism focusing on favoritism toward farmers and rice corruption allegations. But research does not support this attribution. A 2023 simulation ran 17 scenarios of release strategies for two dams and concluded that even with perfect foresight of subsequent rainfall, the flooded area could be reduced by at most 3.68%. A 2020 study examining hydrological stations along the Chao Phraya River found that in one low-lying disaster area, less than 30% of the floodwater came from the river, while 73.7% came from local rainfall. In other words, the water fell directly on the disaster zone; dam decisions cannot bear that blame.

9:25 Why Seagate, untouched by water, also shut down
Seagate's factory in Korat was largely unaffected, but production still stopped—because seven of its top ten suppliers were flooded. A typical case was Japan's Nidec, which makes spindle motors for hard drives; two of its plants were submerged and halted production. The hard drive supply chain is tightly interlocked: no matter how safe the assembly line, if motors don't arrive, the whole line stops. Seagate quickly qualified new suppliers, modified designs to reduce complexity, and negotiated payment terms with suppliers, limiting its quarterly shipment decline to 8%. In the same year, Western Digital's core plant was flooded to a depth of 1.8 meters, and quarterly shipments fell 51%. The difference was not in the height of their buildings but in which company's supply chain could reroute around the break faster.

12:34 Zero inventory amplified the flood into a global shortage
Before the flood, the hard drive industry had just gone through a round of consolidation: Western Digital announced in March 2011 it would acquire Hitachi's hard drive business, and a month later Seagate announced it would acquire Samsung, bringing supply and demand barely back into balance. Because there was no surplus inventory to draw down, the shock was multiplied. Tom Coughlin estimated that Q4 2011 hard drive demand was about 180 million units, but actual production was only 110 to 120 million; and the flood hit right before the Christmas shopping season. Retail prices immediately rose 20% to 40%; a 1TB hard drive at Taipei's Guanghua Digital Plaza went from NT$1,750 to over NT$3,000. Even Intel admitted in December that Q4 revenue would be about $1 billion lower than expected due to the hard drive shortage. A localized flood, amplified by zero inventory, became a global shortage.

15:41 Floodwaters receded, but hard drive prices stayed high for two years
The water receded, but the shortage did not end quickly. Hard drive availability returned to pre-flood levels only about nine months later; retail prices took even longer to fall—Newegg prices did not drop back to pre-flood levels until April 2013. Backblaze calculated from its own purchasing records: in September 2011, cost per GB was $0.044, and it did not return to that level until September 2013. Why is it easier to raise prices than to lower them? The author offers several interpretations: the ecosystem recovered more slowly than expected, the 2011 acquisitions added extra costs, tablets caused a permanent decline in PC hard drive demand, and a more cynical guess—after Seagate and Western Digital acquired second-tier rivals, only three major players remained, making prices easier to 'stabilize,' or, in his words, to cartelize. He does not conclude which is true.

18:47 The flooded giant chose to stay and build more walls
Western Digital's post-disaster choice is telling: it did not retreat but doubled down on defense. WD and the Bang Pa-in estate owner built an 11-kilometer flood wall along the estate, and WD added a 6-meter inner wall around its factory; to add supply chain redundancy, in December 2011 it announced a new slider fab in Malaysia. A survey of 50 directly affected Japanese companies showed that nearly 80% decided to stay in Thailand. The reason is not hard to understand: existing estates, supporting infrastructure, and skilled workers are not easy to pack up and move. Thailand has since faced more major floods, especially in the 2020s, with almost annual occurrences; in November of the most recent year, it even rained what was called a 'once-in-300-years' event, but these estates have held so far. Whether stronger defenses will be needed in the future can only be tested by the next big flood.

item.title: AI Designs Viruses That Infect Bacteria, but Success Rate Is Only 5%
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-twiv-ai-设计出能感染细菌的病毒-但成功率仅-5/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-twiv-ai-设计出能感染细菌的病毒-但成功率仅-5/
item.description: AI has, for the first time, designed complete viral genomes from scratch that can infect bacteria; the experimental validation success rate is only about 5%, far from the all-capable image portrayed in the media.
item.content:encoded:
AI has, for the first time, designed complete viral genomes from scratch that can infect bacteria; the experimental validation success rate is only about 5%, far from the all-capable image portrayed in the media.

This episode breaks down the success rate, compensatory mutations, and biosafety rhetoric of AI-designed viruses, while also demonstrating how observational vaccine studies can be refuted by E-values.

12:43 Vaccine switching as a natural control
The pitfall of the 'healthy vaccinee bias' is that vaccinated individuals tend to be more health-conscious than the unvaccinated, so comparing the two groups can mistake lifestyle differences for vaccine effects. This study exploits the 2017 U.S. switch of the shingles vaccine from Zostavax to Shingrix: those vaccinated before the policy change received the old vaccine, and those after received the new one; both groups were actively vaccinated, theoretically eliminating the bias. However, it is still not a randomized trial; unmeasured factors such as socioeconomic status, smoking, and diet may still be unbalanced between the two groups, so it can only be considered a quasi-experiment.

15:47 Weak confounding can overturn vaccine benefit
How strong must unmeasured confounding be to overturn an observational conclusion? The E-value measures this. This vaccine study has an E-value of only 1.42, almost touching 1, meaning a confounding factor that is not very strong and is associated with both 'which vaccine received' and 'cardiovascular outcome' could explain away the observed risk reduction. An E-value of 3.4 or even 5 would indicate a robust conclusion; 1.42 is far from robust. The authors themselves admit that randomized clinical trials are needed for confirmation, and this observation should not be taken as evidence.

38:13 AI designs functional viral genomes for the first time
The researchers used genomic language models EVO1 and EVO2 to write phage genomes: first training the models on vast amounts of public DNA sequences, then fine-tuning on PhiX174 to generate thousands of candidate sequences. When tested back in the lab, only about 5% of the products could actually infect E. coli. This is the first time AI has designed complete genomes from scratch that are proven functional. Media summaries that say 'AI directly creates viruses' miss a key point: the models only see sequences, with no experimental annotations telling them which base does what, and the 5% hit rate shows they are still largely ignorant of how sequence determines function.

44:37 Replication origin is the model's most conserved memory
The prompt to the model only needed the first 4 to 9 nucleotides of the PhiX174 genome, and the accuracy of the generated results increased significantly. The authors found that this unassuming sequence is part of the replication origin and is 100% conserved across all genomes generated by the model. It acts like a 'I am a real virus' password: the model locks the replication origin as a core element that must be preserved, while allowing other positions to evolve freely. This also explains why such a short prompt is effective—the key is not the length of the prompt but whether it hits a functional Achilles' heel.

56:55 AI swaps a gene and adds 58 mutations on its own
The design of EVO36 is not a full rewrite but a gene swap: replacing the J gene of PhiX174 with the shorter J protein from phage G4. In the past, when humans performed the same transplant manually, the product could not infect; but the AI-generated EVO36 infects normally because it accumulated an additional 58 mutations across the genome. These mutations appear to be compensatory mutations that allow the foreign J protein to re-adapt to the local environment. Humans might not think to change 58 positions at once, which is where generative models surpass single-point editing.

1:00:15 Phage cocktails target drug-resistant bacteria
Natural PhiX174 hits a wall when encountering already resistant bacteria, failing to break through even after five passages; a mixture of 16 AI-synthesized phages infects the originally resistant strains within one or two passages. The resistance is not broken by a single phage but by several synthetic phages recombining during replication, accumulating new mutations, and finally breaching the barrier through collective cooperation. This result suggests that phage therapy should not bet on a single strain but rather use a cocktail of multiple synthetic phages.

1:07:29 Don't frame AI-made viruses as an urgent threat
For the study generating PhiX174, a commentary in the same issue used the word 'urgent' to describe its biosafety implications. Vincent directly opposed this wording on the show: the authors have already demonstrated through reproducible experiments that such research can be done safely, so the real task is not to sound the alarm but to start building a safety framework. He also emphasized that reconstructing viruses is not science fiction as long as the sequence is available, and precisely for that reason we need frameworks rather than panic.

1:35:53 Not vaccinating is often just not knowing
When discussing people who do not get vaccinated, the article raises an often-overlooked mechanism: some people do not vaccinate not out of religious or ideological opposition but simply because they do not know they should. Treating all vaccine hesitancy as a 'belief issue' misdirects policy—for these people, the key is not debate or persuasion but information outreach so they first learn the vaccine exists.

item.title: Sports Betting Seeps Into Gen Z, Financial Regulatory Risk Underestimated
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-excessreturns-体育博彩渗透z世代-金融监管风险被低估/
