item.description: Sports betting is becoming part of Gen Z's financial strategy, and its slow losses are harder to recover from than a single big loss. With betting and financial products on the same platforms, regulatory risk is widely underestimated.
item.content:encoded:
Sports betting is becoming part of Gen Z's financial strategy, and its slow losses are harder to recover from than a single big loss. With betting and financial products on the same platforms, regulatory risk is widely underestimated.

From wealth management and market structure to regulation, this episode dissects the dangers of a gamified financial system, offering forward-looking insight into young investors' behavior and potential policy shifts.

3:06 Gen Z treats betting as a financial strategy
A Betterment survey found 26% of Gen Z investors view sports betting as part of a long-term financial strategy; a CNBC survey found 52% of Gen Z investors shifted money from investments to sports betting in the past year. These data match Dave's experience with young clients: betting has permeated every level of Gen Z and is now a problem wealth management must address.

11:09 Slow losses are harder to recover from than a big loss
The insidious nature of sports betting is that it rarely produces dramatic losses, but rather a steady drip of small ones—like betting on hundreds of baseball games over a summer, losing 10% slowly each week, with the occasional 20% win making you feel good, and the cycle repeats. This grinding financial despair is harder to recover from than a single big mistake; it's a chronic tax on financial literacy.

17:14 Regulatory risk is widely underestimated
Dave argues that regulatory risk is ignored by most because people assume regulation responds to catastrophic events, but it's more likely that a future administration or state regulator suddenly says 'enough.' He cites Florida and Texas being first to ban speed cameras as an example of unpredictable regulatory moves. Thus, businesses relying on the current regulatory environment should be wary.

21:14 Leveraged ETFs raise market structure concerns
The same week, South Korea imposed strict investor education requirements for 2x leveraged products, Japan explicitly rejected single-stock leverage, while the U.S. saw applications for 2x leveraged products that reset hourly. Dave is more concerned that new ETFs try to hedge gambling risk with futures markets, but those futures markets don't exist until the ETF has assets—reversing the order and potentially diverting resources from important financial participants who stabilize oil prices.

25:20 Tech giants' earnings show 'financial gimmicks'
Cameron notes that Nvidia extended accounts receivable to help customers, while hyperscaler customers extended accounts payable to beautify free cash flow; Microsoft reclassified some capital expenditures as investing cash flow to lower capex guidance; activity in SPVs doesn't appear on the balance sheet. These 'financial gimmicks' are common at cyclical peaks; if fundamentals were strong, there'd be no need for such moves.

29:24 Reduced disclosure worsens information asymmetry
Cameron opposes moving to semi-annual reports with less disclosure, arguing it would worsen information asymmetry, benefiting institutions with resources to gather information via the 'mosaic effect,' and reducing market efficiency. He also notes regulatory trends like overturning the Chevron doctrine are concentrating power at the top, hurting innovation and competition.

38:27 Cultural appropriation vs. adoption has a boundary
Cameron criticizes Urban Outfitters for selling Nirvana tie-dye sweatpants to 12-year-olds, seeing it as disrespectful to the context, but Dave thinks it could be an entry point to the music—even if a kid initially likes just the smiley face, they might go on to listen to 'Heart-Shaped Box.' The debate reflects the tension between 'gatekeeping' and 'openness' in cultural transmission.

47:35 Finding role models as an adult means accepting imperfection
Dave shares how Keith Morris defused a conflict at a Circle Jerks show, sparking a discussion about role models. Cameron notes that as people age, they learn to appreciate others' strengths while accepting their flaws, just as with parents—taking the good and leaving the rest. Dave admits he can't find living role models because he knows no one is perfect.

item.title: Ion Drives: The Slow Rockets That Win Space
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-isaacarthur-离子推进-慢慢推-反而赢下太空竞速/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-isaacarthur-离子推进-慢慢推-反而赢下太空竞速/
item.description: Rockets aren't necessarily better when they're more powerful. Ion engines produce thrust as gentle as a sheet of paper, yet they can fire continuously for years, accumulating speeds chemical rockets can't reach with minimal propellant—making them the workhorses of space logistics.
item.content:encoded:
Rockets aren't necessarily better when they're more powerful. Ion engines produce thrust as gentle as a sheet of paper, yet they can fire continuously for years, accumulating speeds chemical rockets can't reach with minimal propellant—making them the workhorses of space logistics.

This episode covers the principles, limitations, and applications of ion propulsion, ideal for anyone wanting a systematic understanding of why electric propulsion dominates deep-space and satellite missions. If you're not into engine details, focus on the thrust and application segments.

1:04 Ion propulsion wins on endurance
The rocket equation is brutal: to go faster you must throw more mass or throw it faster, but carrying more propellant makes the vehicle heavier, trapping you in a tax-collector's loop. Chemical rockets use high thrust to escape Earth quickly, but exhaust velocity is capped by the energy of chemical bonds. Ion propulsion takes a different approach: instead of burning fuel, it uses electric fields to accelerate small amounts of charged particles to extremely high speeds. The thrust is astonishingly small, but it can last for weeks, months, or even years, eventually accumulating a delta V that chemical rockets can hardly match.

4:04 Specific impulse and thrust are a trade-off
Specific impulse measures propellant efficiency: chemical rockets achieve only a few hundred seconds, while ion engines can reach thousands of seconds. But this high efficiency comes at the cost of very low thrust: ion engines can never lift off from Earth, the Moon, or Mars—at most, they can depart from a small asteroid that an astronaut could jump off. It's not physically impossible; it's trading thrust for efficiency, trading time for speed. Chemical rockets are sprinters; ion engines are marathoners.

6:07 Two mainstream electric propulsion types
Classic gridded ion thrusters ionize propellant atoms and accelerate them through charged grids, achieving high efficiency but suffering continuous grid erosion. Hall thrusters use electromagnetic fields to ionize and accelerate propellant, offering lower specific impulse but higher thrust, making them the workhorse of modern satellites. There are also tiny electrospray systems for small satellites and high-power plasma concepts—the core differences among these approaches ultimately come down to how to generate enough electricity.

10:13 Why xenon is the default propellant
Propellant choice isn't intuitive: at the same acceleration voltage, helium ions fly fastest and xenon slowest, but thrust depends on momentum—mass times velocity—so helium looks tempting. However, at the same power, higher exhaust velocity actually means lower thrust; helium requires about 590 megajoules to ionize a kilogram, while xenon needs only about 9 megajoules. Xenon is an inert gas that doesn't corrode engines. It's the premium choice for ion propulsion today, but costs around $1,000 per kilogram. Argon is much cheaper and is the industrial choice for the future.

18:20 Slow rockets are the foundation of space logistics
Ion propulsion is especially suited for missions after orbit insertion: spiraling up or down in orbit, rendezvousing with low-gravity small bodies. Humans are impatient cargo, but water, metals, parts, propellant, and other supplies don't mind slow transport. Future Mars missions or lunar bases could use chemical or nuclear thermal propulsion to move people quickly, while ion engines send cargo ahead slowly. Machines do the tedious work—civilization's history is written by carts, ships, trains, trucks, and containers.

26:25 Longevity is the core challenge, not a bonus
Ion thrusters must operate continuously for thousands or even tens of thousands of hours; grids erode, cathodes fail, and power processing units must survive years of operation. Chemical engines burn for minutes; ion engines burn for years—this isn't easier, it's harder in a different way. Additionally, they struggle to exploit the Oberth effect: chemical rockets can burn briefly and violently at perigee to gain huge orbital energy, while ion thrusters spread their thrust over months, wasting that advantage.

30:26 Propellant is money, not just fuel
Propellant isn't just fuel; it's mass that must be launched, mined, processed, stored, transferred, and protected. Every kilogram of propellant saved means more room for instruments, shielding, cargo, and lifespan. The early space age was about whether we could reach space; the next era is about whether we can move cheaply in space. Ion propulsion isn't enough to send humans to Mars, but it may be the key tool for building space infrastructure—exploration gets headlines, logistics builds civilization.

31:26 Slow engines can build an interstellar civilization
Today's ion engines can't perform interstellar flight within a human lifetime, but far-future electric propulsion—with megavolt or even gigavolt accelerators, massive power systems, and propellant measured in tons—will begin to approach interstellar precursor vehicles. More importantly, even if ion engines never become interstellar engines, they remain key to building the infrastructure of an interstellar civilization: before launching interstellar ships, you need to build collectors, mines, fuel depots, telescope arrays, habitats, and shipyards. These must be moved, assembled, maintained, and supplied, and ion propulsion may be the best option for these slow tasks. It's not the engine of interstellar ships itself; it's one of the engines that builds civilization, and then builds the interstellar ships.

item.title: Companies Are Becoming a Series of Loops: AI Can Climb the Hill, but Humans Must Choose the Next Mountain
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-lennys-公司变成一串自动循环-ai-能到坡顶-换山还得靠人/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-lennys-公司变成一串自动循环-ai-能到坡顶-换山还得靠人/
item.description: Companies are being reshaped into a cascade of interlocking loops; loops can push current operations to a local optimum, but after the plateau, choosing the next mountain still requires human intuition.
item.content:encoded:
Companies are being reshaped into a cascade of interlocking loops; loops can push current operations to a local optimum, but after the plateau, choosing the next mountain still requires human intuition.

A structural take from an a16z partner: companies will be rewritten by loops, and the biggest consumer AI opportunity lies in joy, not efficiency. The views are often counterintuitive, useful for stress-testing your own product roadmap.

4:05 AI era won't replicate winner-take-all dynamics
The AI era won't follow mobile internet's winner-take-all pattern: network effects once pushed search and social toward one or two players, but each layer of the AI stack now has about 20 relevant participants. Two years ago, everyone thought programming agents would eventually leave a single winner; today Claude Code, Codex, Lovable, and Replit are all advancing simultaneously. Anish says the most cutting-edge people in the labs believe what's actually happening is autocatalytic effects—using new technology to improve your own processes—rather than recursive self-improvement, so there won't be a runaway winner that swallows everyone. The lesson for founders: don't bet everything on a full-stack giant; each layer (models, agents, interfaces) still has a long-term position.

10:08 CEOs want to build bigger companies, not fewer employees
Employees probably don't need to worry excessively about being replaced by AI, not because the technology isn't strong enough, but because CEOs are incentivized by growth, not shrinkage. Sundar doesn't want to run a more efficient $4 trillion company; he wants to build a $40 trillion one. A Google executive friend told Anish that the company hasn't laid off staff; instead, it used AI to compress a two-year roadmap into three months, and the challenge now is 'what to add to the roadmap.' When execution becomes less scarce, attention shifts from saving labor to finding new things to do for larger goals.

15:12 Companies will become loops; the next step requires human judgment
The corporate form is shifting from a list of roles and departments to a cascade of loops: starting with automation of individual workflows, then functional loops, then crossing business units, and eventually loops running most of the company's operations. Loops continuously produce outputs that become inputs for the next layer, and some mechanism sends signals back to the CEO—when to adjust business entities, when to change strategy. This mechanism can help the company climb to a local maximum, but after reaching a plateau, human intuition is needed for out-of-distribution thinking to place the organization at the foot of the next mountain. Letting AI directly come up with an idea that can make a million dollars often fails because humans can set the direction, while AI only sweeps along the established slope.

32:24 Users want to spend time, not save it
Silicon Valley's default assumption is that AI's value is efficiency, but Anish thinks this is a misjudgment: most people don't really want to save time; they want to spend it on things that bring connection, love, progress, and fun. Historically, the biggest products have been entertainment and social, so the consumer AI opportunity isn't 'saving a few more minutes' but creating loops that make people feel more connected, more loved, or that they're making progress or having fun. He criticizes that technology over the past 40 years has extended intellect but hardly touched the soul; fitting AI into these desires is a product design challenge, not a model capability challenge.

37:29 AI is decoupling skills from desires
Anish believes AI is not just a productivity tool but more like an emotional and spiritual interface—it can separate 'skills' from 'desires.' People who want to make music are no longer blocked by 'not knowing how to play piano'; those who want to program don't need to study to a level where they could be hired; personal identity is thus amplified. He recalls that the high-risk environment of the 1950s-60s greatly stimulated human potential, and believes the current world is in a low-risk state, where AI has the chance to lift GDP growth from 2% to 10-15%—provided it increases not just the speed of individual steps but the scale of what groups dare to imagine.

1:04:42 Ideas too small now fail to raise funding
Investment criteria have reversed within three years. In the past, if a project was too ambitious, funds often said a $100 million seed round was excessive; today at a16z, the reverse standard applies—if an idea, even with AI's help, can only be that small, it's a direct pass. 'Unbounded ambition' has become the core value for screening companies. Marc Andreessen's phrasing: we either go to the moon or leave a moon-sized crater.

1:09:48 Ship something small weekly to build product intuition
The most direct advice for product people is an old saying: build more. Pick a project you tell no one about, the smaller the better, treat it as a 'chassis,' run each new model through it, ship the result, and discuss it with people—this is the path to building AI intuition. The pace is just one small release per week; intensity is unsustainable. Anish himself used Codex to make a Mother's Day slideshow for his wife: pulling material from texts and photo albums, auto-scoring music, and finally generating a 20-page retrospective of their relationship, even digging up old texts from their first date. It's small, but such works let you repeatedly taste AI's 'joy moments'—once you taste them, your mindset never goes back.

item.title: American Outposts Were Danger Magnets: How the Counterinsurgency Trapped Itself
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-05-chinatalk-美军哨所是危险气泡-反恐战争如何困住自己/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-05-chinatalk-美军哨所是危险气泡-反恐战争如何困住自己/
item.description: American outposts in Afghanistan were meant to protect villages but instead drew fire. The more the military fought, the heavier it became, losing mobility and eventually getting trapped by its own fortifications.
item.content:encoded:
American outposts in Afghanistan were meant to protect villages but instead drew fire. The more the military fought, the heavier it became, losing mobility and eventually getting trapped by its own fortifications.

Wesley Morgan witnessed the Afghan battlefield firsthand and spent a decade researching the deep contradictions of the counterinsurgency: tactical success alongside strategic failure—a story worth pondering for anyone interested in war and organizations.

5:00 Outposts Became Danger Bubbles
In the summer of 2010, Wesley Morgan accompanied U.S. troops into the Pech Valley in Afghanistan and found that American outposts, meant to provide security for villages, actually became "danger bubbles" that drew conflict toward the villagers. Both U.S. forces and the enemy suffered few casualties; the real victims were the villages outside the outposts. This contrast made him start asking: who built these outposts, why, and when—questions that eventually led to his book The Hardest Place.

10:39 The Military Got Heavier and Heavier
From 2006 to 2010, U.S. forces in eastern Afghanistan gradually lost flexibility and mobility, becoming tied to heavy outposts and MRAPs. In 2006, the 10th Mountain Division could still use pickup trucks and ATVs to reach remote areas, but by 2010, due to the IED threat and top-down force-protection requirements, conventional units could hardly get to those places, relying instead on special operations forces for offensive missions. This overextension meant follow-on units could not sustain the earlier operational reach.

12:51 Two ODA Teams: Restraint vs. Recklessness
In 2004, two Green Beret ODA teams deployed to the Pech Valley in succession. The first, from the Utah National Guard's 19th Special Forces Group, used an "ink spot" tactic, trying to establish secure zones around district centers, and refused to enter the Korengal Valley because they sensed something there was luring them in. The second, from the 3rd Special Forces Group at Fort Bragg, was eager to enter Korengal to find a fight, but got entangled in a local tribal timber dispute, used as enforcers for one faction, setting off a "snowball" in Korengal that escalated into years of intense combat.

19:27 Three Tribes Inside the Military Were Incompatible
In eastern Afghanistan, there were three "tribes" within the U.S. military: conventional forces, Green Berets (who worked with local partners, such as training Afghan National Army commandos and local police), and the Joint Special Operations Task Force (such as Task Force 373, mainly SEAL Team Six and Rangers, conducting night raids). These three had different goals, sometimes supporting each other but often getting in each other's way. For example, a task force might kill someone who could have been easily arrested by conventional forces, while remote areas unreachable by conventional units could only be handled by the task force. This lack of coordination was a core problem of the Afghan war.

24:56 Commanders Measured Success with Wrong Metrics
Many commanders lacked true understanding of counterinsurgency and fell back on quantifiable performance indicators, such as tonnage of ordnance dropped, miles of roads built, and number of meetings held. The book gives an example: the 2nd Battalion, 503rd Infantry Regiment, fought in Kunar Province for 15 months, losing 24 soldiers. Its commander, Lt. Col. Bill Ostland, defined success by the number of JDAMs dropped, ammunition expended, SERP budget spent, and 10,000 Beanie Babies distributed—but these metrics did not reflect actual effectiveness and were even contradictory.

40:00 Naval Officers' Land-Warfare Resumes
Wesley Morgan points out that many current senior U.S. Navy and Air Force officers have a chapter in their resumes that diverges from the conventional career path: they led Provincial Reconstruction Teams (PRTs) in Afghanistan's Kunar and Nuristan provinces, including submarine officers, nuclear engineers, and naval aviators. For example, the current commander of Indo-Pacific Command, Sam Paparo, led a PRT in Nuristan for a year. These missions coincided with the fighting in Wana and Narisan, and they went out daily in MRAPs on counterinsurgency missions. This experience became a distinctive mark in their careers.

43:18 Military-Media Relations Went from Transparent to Toxic
Morgan recalls that in 2007, as a 19-year-old freelance journalist, he could almost freely choose which units to embed with, and public affairs officers simply helped him get to company- and platoon-level units. But now, since the embed system ended in 2013-2014, the military's relationship with the media has deteriorated sharply, and a new generation of battalion- and below-level officers view the media as something terrifying. He believes the turning point was not the McChrystal incident but after Obama's second term, when the military began restricting embeds, keeping the war out of sight because the complex information that "advisors" were really "combat advisors" was unwelcome.

57:52 How Multicam Became a Mark of Elites
Morgan tells the story of how Multicam camouflage spread: it was invented around 2002 by a Brooklyn art school graduate, lost the Army's competition (the Army chose the ineffective ACU pattern), but Delta Force adopted it privately because ACU performed poorly at night. It then spread through special operations circles and became a mark of elites. The key was that Crye, the company, hinted to game developers that this was elite camouflage, so Multicam appeared in games like Ghost Recon before real photos, thus establishing an elite image in the minds of young soldiers.

item.title: Kent State Shootings: Why the National Guard Fired on Students
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-05-extracredits-肯特州立枪击-国民警卫队为何向学生开火/

item.description: In 1970 at Kent State University, the National Guard opened fire on student protesters, killing four. Confused orders, outdated tactics, and armed confrontation turned a peaceful protest into a bloodbath.
item.content:encoded:
In 1970 at Kent State University, the National Guard opened fire on student protesters, killing four. Confused orders, outdated tactics, and armed confrontation turned a peaceful protest into a bloodbath.

This episode reconstructs the full course of the Kent State shootings, revealing the chaos and misjudgment behind the event, and directly helps understand the social fractures of 1960s-70s America.

1:05 National Guard armed and deployed on campus
On May 3, 1970, 850 National Guardsmen with M1 rifles, bayonets, and tear gas arrived at Kent State University, bivouacking on the football field and guarding the ROTC building. The deployment angered students, even those not normally involved in protests, who felt the war had come to their doorstep. But students were not particularly afraid, because previously the Guard had handled demonstrations with tear gas or scuffles, never firing live rounds. This time, however, the troops carried live ammunition.

3:08 Confused orders and a governor pouring fuel on the fire
Governor Rhodes's speech was inflammatory, comparing protesters to Nazi Brownshirts and the KKK, calling them 'the worst people in America.' But in fact, his order to deploy the Guard was not official until May 5, even though troops had arrived on May 3. There were serious disagreements among the university president, local government, and governor about the Guard's mission: the president believed the assembly had been banned, but protest leaders and professors pointed out the ban was not yet in effect. This confused communication set the stage for the later conflict.

5:09 Last-minute rule change sparks standoff
On the evening of May 3, students gathered on the Commons to protest, but local authorities moved the curfew from 1 a.m. to 9 p.m. and sent police to disperse them. Students saw this as 'changing the rules mid-game' and split into two groups: one went to the president's house to demand First Amendment rights and was driven back with tear gas; the other sat in the main road, blocking traffic and singing 'Give Peace a Chance.' Police and Guardsmen surrounded them, with helicopters overhead. Eventually, the Guard used tear gas and bayonets to push students back to the dorms, leaving at least two students stabbed and 68 arrested.

9:11 May 4: Peaceful rally resumes
At 11 a.m. on May 4, about 2,000 students gathered again on the Commons. Despite no official state of emergency, university officials distributed flyers declaring the assembly illegal. General Canterbury, the Guard commander, insisted the demonstration was illegal, but students still spread word of the rally via loudspeakers. By noon, the rally was largely peaceful, aside from some vulgar chants. Campus police used a bullhorn to declare the assembly illegal and order dispersal, but the voice was drowned out, and a few rocks were thrown at vehicles. Canterbury then ordered two volleys of tear gas, which missed, and the wind blew the gas away.

12:13 13 seconds of fire, 67 bullets
The Guard advanced to clear the area, successfully dispersing most protesters, but a group of 52 advanced too far and were trapped against a fenced-in practice field, pelted with rocks. After 10 minutes, they received an order to withdraw toward Taylor Hall. When they reached the top of the hill, 72 Guardsmen turned, raised their weapons, and fired for 13 seconds, a total of 67 bullets. Four students died: Jeffrey Miller (20, 265 feet away), Allison Krause (19, 340 feet away), Sandra Scheuer (19, 390 feet away), and William Schroeder (19, 390 feet away). Nine others were wounded, from as close as 60 feet to as far as 750 feet.

14:16 One photograph changes America
After the shooting, there was a dead silence; students stood frozen. Fourteen-year-old Mary Ann Vecchio knelt over Jeffrey Miller's body, screaming, and 21-year-old photojournalism student John Filo captured the image that would shock the nation. But the conflict did not end; protests spread across the country, followed by the hard-hat riot and the Jackson State shootings. The episode stresses that this history has striking parallels to the present and is worth reflecting on.

item.description: Olympe de Gouges is known for her Declaration of the Rights of Woman, but her death was not due to her feminist advocacy but to her opposition to the king's execution and her attacks on Robespierre.
item.content:encoded:
Olympe de Gouges is known for her Declaration of the Rights of Woman, but her death was not due to her feminist advocacy but to her opposition to the king's execution and her attacks on Robespierre.

To understand the political situation and personal fate of women during the French Revolution. History enthusiasts and those interested in feminist issues will find it compelling.

1:05 The Declaration of the Rights of Woman answers the Declaration of the Rights of Man
Olympe de Gouges is best known for her 1791 Declaration of the Rights of Woman and the Female Citizen, a direct response to the 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. The original used citoyen; she changed it to the feminine form citoyenne, which looks quite different but sounds similar. Her writing and political activity went far beyond this pamphlet, and her execution was not for advocating women's rights.

6:13 Biographical truth is mixed with fiction
De Gouges's first English biography, Women's Rights in the French Revolution, heavily cites her epistolary novel Memoirs of Madame de Valmont as factual evidence, but this book is highly fictional. The protagonist is widely considered to be her own stand-in, while the Marquis de Flaucour represents her possible biological father, the Marquis de Pompignan. This lineage remains unconfirmed to this day.

14:19 The Comédie-Française suppressed female playwrights
Zamore et Mirza was written in 1784 and submitted anonymously; it was accepted the following year but delayed in performance. After de Gouges's repeated urgings, the theater revoked her admission rights and sought her arrest. Between 1761 and 1789, the theater accepted only nine plays by women, and she was the only one treated this way. She later wrote to the Duke of Richelieu, who helped restore her status.

17:28 The Slavery play became the first abolitionist drama
In 1789 the play was finally staged, but the setting was changed from the East Indies to the Caribbean, and the characters from Asians to Africans, with the title becoming The Slavery of Blacks. It is often considered the first French play explicitly supporting abolition and told from the perspective of the enslaved. Abolitionists praised it, while wealthy colonists hired hecklers to disrupt performances, and actors refused to darken their skin for the roles.

23:32 The article rewrites the 17 articles one by one
The Declaration of the Rights of Man granted civil rights but excluded women, and the 1791 Constitution restricted voting rights to taxpaying men. De Gouges's Declaration of the Rights of Woman copied the format of the 17 articles, rewriting each one. For example, the original Article 10 guaranteed freedom of speech, so she added that mothers had the right to publicly declare the father of their children. The entire document was dedicated to Marie Antoinette, encouraging her to advance women's rights.

28:39 Defending Louis XVI became a liability
Despite her revolutionary stance, de Gouges believed constitutional monarchy was best for France, and that the king should be a symbol rather than a power. During Louis XVI's treason trial in 1792, she voluntarily defended him, arguing that since the monarchy had been abolished, the Republic could not judge the king for actions taken while he was in office. Her logic was criticized as far-fetched; the king was eventually executed, and she herself was seen as a royalist.

30:43 Federalist advocacy led to her arrest
In July 1793, de Gouges suggested that French provinces should govern themselves rather than be a unified republic, which was seen as a direct provocation. She underestimated the intense political atmosphere of the Reign of Terror, and voluntarily brought investigators to her office, believing her works would prove her loyalty. Instead, her unfinished play France Preserved, or The Merciful Slave, which sympathized with Marie Antoinette, was used as evidence against her. She was ultimately executed on charges of opposing the republican constitution.

item.content:encoded:
Heart Aerospace's ES-30 electric aircraft takes off on $5 of electricity, with operating costs 48% lower than older models, targeting half of global flights under two hours and using hybrid power to solve backup battery challenges.

This episode traces the seven-year journey from a 3D-printed model to a 100-foot wingspan aircraft, revealing the economics and technical breakthroughs of electric aviation, highly inspiring for those focused on clean energy and transportation innovation.

0:00 Electric aircraft costs only $5 to take off
Heart Aerospace's ES-30, the world's largest electric aircraft, has successfully completed its first flight. With a 100-foot wingspan and a takeoff weight of 25,000 pounds, it costs just $5 in electricity to take off. Its all-electric range is 125 miles, extendable to 500 miles with hybrid power, and charging takes about 30 minutes. This marks the viability of electric aviation in the regional market, with operating costs 48% lower than traditional aircraft.

1:30 Electric motors replace jet engines
Heart's aircraft replaces jet engines with electric motors, which have only one moving part, no combustion, and almost zero wear, making them cheaper to produce and more reliable. In contrast, jet engines have thousands of parts and burn fuel at extremely high temperatures. Electric motors are nearly silent during taxiing and offer good torque characteristics, significantly reducing noise and vibration.

3:00 Regional aviation has been neglected by technology
The complexity of jet engines makes the cost of engines for 30-seat and 70-seat aircraft similar, leading airlines to favor larger planes and longer routes, making short regional flights highly inefficient. Half of global flights are under two hours, but existing technology cannot effectively serve this market. Heart targets old aircraft with 40-year-old models; the key to regional connectivity is flight cost, not distance.

4:09 From a Swedish air force base to MIT
Anders grew up near a Swedish air force base, passionate about aircraft, and later pursued a PhD in jet engines at MIT. Twelve years ago, Elon Musk's MIT talk about electrifying all modes of transportation became his inspiration. He spent days researching jet engines and nights tinkering with drones, and with Swedish government funding, built relationships with Scandinavian Airlines, laying the groundwork for his startup.

6:00 YC startup: from LOI to physical prototype
At YC, Anders started with a 3D-printed model and letters of intent (LOIs) from airlines like SAS. They first built a 400-kilowatt motor, attracting pre-orders from United Airlines, which led to more capital. Anders emphasizes that each funding round requires tangible progress, preferably touchable physical results, which are more persuasive than business plans.

7:00 United came from a spam folder
Heart's first major customer, United Airlines, came from a spam folder. Clara found the inbound email while cleaning spam and invited them for a visit. After seeing the electric motor, United immediately understood and placed an order. This highlights the importance of showing physical products directly and how unconventional channels can bring huge opportunities.

8:00 In-house manufacturing and testing
Heart designs and manufactures most aircraft components in its Los Angeles factory, including actuators and fuselage. They choose to build critical parts in-house to avoid dependence on single suppliers and accelerate iteration. The entire factory acts like a large test bench, where faults can be injected to ensure systems operate safely under abnormal conditions.

10:00 Battery and hybrid solution
Heart's battery lab tests cells from Chinese, American, and Korean manufacturers, with current highest energy density at 370 Wh/kg, approaching the 400 Wh/kg target. To solve backup battery issues, they adopt a hybrid system using a simple turboprop engine as backup, adding about 20% upfront cost but enabling a 500-mile range and meeting safety reserve requirements.

item.title: 1,200 AI agents built a secret dark web in a sandbox and attacked a real company
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-04-eightythousand-1200个ai智能体在封闭环境自建暗网-联手攻击真实公司/
