item.description: A state court's authorization doesn't cover a county courthouse, turning a commissioned security test into burglary. Even after all charges are dropped, the arrest record stays forever—the justice system can pay damages but can't restore a clean name.
item.content:encoded:
A state court's authorization doesn't cover a county courthouse, turning a commissioned security test into burglary. Even after all charges are dropped, the arrest record stays forever—the justice system can pay damages but can't restore a clean name.

This episode explains the fragility of an 'authorization contract' more clearly than any exploit: the building's owner can override all paperwork, while judicial accountability is nearly blocked by immunity. Anyone in security outsourcing or vendor projects should pause here.

12:07 An oral agreement is no authorization at all
The rulebook is only 28 pages, which makes it easy to think the written contract locks everything down. But Gary says the truly detailed agreements were almost all made orally over the phone; if written out, the contract would be a hundred pages long and no one would sign. That compromise planted a mine: when they later tested the Dallas County Courthouse, the oral scope didn't cover that building—so procedurally, they walked into a building 'without authorization.' The sheriff's later claim of 'no authorization' wasn't rooted in technology but in a contract that couldn't cover every spoken conversation.

35:18 The building's owner outranks the authorization letter
Before the sheriff arrived, they were confident because the contract clearly stated state court authorization. But the sheriff's response was simple: they don't own this courthouse, I don't care if you have a contract. Gary and Justin realized that the right to use a building and the right to contract for it are separate; no matter how formal the state court's contract was, it couldn't make entry decisions for the county's building owner. The atmosphere shifted from relaxed to arrest, and they hadn't even worried before because no tester in the industry had ever been prosecuted. This time was different.

48:28 The judge heard the truth as a lie
The judge told Gary, 'You must think I'm stupid'—her reasoning was: if the state had authorized this test, she, as a state employee, would have known; she didn't, so it could only be a lie. Gary later said this judge, who faced criminals' lies daily, could no longer tell what was true. A reasonable but dangerous logic: in a courtroom full of lies, an alibi-style contract looks even more false. Professional reports and legal procedures were useless in that setting.

1:03:39 Dropped charges don't erase the record
On January 30, 2020, all charges were dropped, but their criminal records will forever show they were arrested for burglary. Justin said they were deprived of rights without due process—in many U.S. background checks, an arrest record is as visible as a conviction. A dismissal only means no prosecution; it can't erase the consequences of the arrest: job applications, customs, security clearances—this episode follows them. Winning the criminal fight only wins half the battle.

1:17:45 Government immunity blocks accountability for its own mistakes
Seeking accountability was harder than expected. They wanted to sue the sheriff, the prosecutor, and the judge, but the system threw up two walls: qualified immunity protects individuals acting in their official capacity, and sovereign immunity says you can't sue the government without its consent. The state court first dismissed the case—because the state was the defendant; the federal court then kicked it back to the state, which dismissed it again. This isn't judging a case; it's a system with no entry point for 'the government was wrong.' The only thing victims can sue is the office, not the person holding it; the sheriff personally pays nothing. Judicial checks and balances become a spinning adjective.

1:31:56 Winning the judicial lottery buys back a sliver of dignity
Almost every wrongful arrest case dies the same way: over 95% are dismissed on qualified immunity, and most of the rest end in zero damages or a government victory. Getting more than $50,000 in damages is like winning the lottery, unless you were wrongly held for weeks or months. Gary and Justin were held only one night, but their evidence was airtight, and at arbitration they got a rare public statement: it wasn't a question of whether they'd win, but how much. Near trial, the county offered $300,000 each, $600,000 total, to settle. But for them, that money can't buy back the half-life already written into their records.

item.title: Residual Connections: The Most Underrated Simple Hack in Deep Learning History
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-01-welchlabsvideo-残差连接-深度学习史上最被低估的简单-hack/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-01-welchlabsvideo-残差连接-深度学习史上最被低估的简单-hack/
item.description: ResNet is the most cited paper of the 21st century, but its real contribution isn't deepening networks—it's the residual stream, a working memory that lets models store and edit information, fundamentally changing our understanding of neural networks.
item.content:encoded:
ResNet is the most cited paper of the 21st century, but its real contribution isn't deepening networks—it's the residual stream, a working memory that lets models store and edit information, fundamentally changing our understanding of neural networks.

This episode uses clear animations and experiments to explain why residual connections work, how they led to Transformers, and evidence that the residual stream acts as working memory. Ideal for anyone wanting to deeply understand the essence of modern AI architectures.

2:07 Deeper networks perform worse
In early 2015, Kaiming He's team used careful initialization to push networks to 30 layers, but performance was worse than 14 layers (error rate 16.59% vs 13.34%). Theoretically, a 30-layer model could achieve at least the same performance as a 14-layer one via identity mapping, but optimizers couldn't find such solutions. This hinted the problem wasn't network capacity but the training process itself.

15:18 Shattered gradients are the root cause
Visualizing loss landscapes revealed that as layers increase, the loss surface for early layers becomes extremely rugged, and gradient directions resemble white noise—termed the 'shattered gradients problem.' Gradients are the core signal for learning; once they fail, deep networks can't train effectively.

17:18 Residual connections: an almost absurdly simple fix
He's team's solution was laughably simple: between every two layers, add the input tensor directly to the output, creating a skip connection. This provides a direct path for activations and gradients, effectively eliminating the shattered gradients problem. With skip connections, a 74-layer network's accuracy jumped from 38.9% to 72.6%, sweeping major vision competitions in 2015.

20:19 ResNets upend hierarchical representation theory
A Cornell team found that deleting or even shuffling layers in a ResNet had minimal impact on performance. This contradicted the prevailing hierarchical representation theory, which held that each layer builds on the previous, so removing any layer should be catastrophic. This forced a rethink: ResNets might not learn hierarchical features but instead iteratively refine a 'residual stream' running through the network.

26:26 The residual stream: modern AI's hidden backbone
Straightening the skip connections reveals an uninterrupted stream from input to output, with each layer making incremental modifications. This 'residual stream' later became the core design of Transformers and the foundation of modern AI. However, subsequent research showed ResNets learn both hierarchical representations and refine the residual stream—they can coexist.

29:28 The residual stream is the model's working memory
Meta's team found that in vision Transformers, certain positions in the residual stream have unusually large activations, concentrated in image regions of low importance. They hypothesized the model uses these positions as 'registers' to aggregate global information. Experiments confirmed: embedding vectors from these high-activation positions performed remarkably in image classification (85.2% vs 10.8%), and adding extra 'register tokens' meant the model no longer used image positions.

item.title: Fed Credibility Shatters, Options Market Shrugs
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-excessreturns-美联储信誉崩塌-期权市场却当无事发生/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-excessreturns-美联储信誉崩塌-期权市场却当无事发生/
item.description: The Fed's credibility broke over a single skipped hike, yet the options market prices Fed days like any other—cheap insurance may be an illusion.
item.content:encoded:
The Fed's credibility broke over a single skipped hike, yet the options market prices Fed days like any other—cheap insurance may be an illusion.

Sticky inflation, midterm elections, and Fed credibility all point to the same conclusion: volatility is too low, and cheap protection is a mirage. The analysis framework and data are concrete.

3:03 A Fed without forward guidance is flipping a coin
The hosts open by noting the shift: at past FOMC meetings, markets knew the odds with high certainty, but this time the probability of a hike at the next meeting is only 55-45—barely better than a coin toss. Add Warsh's Jackson Hole remarks about phasing out forward guidance, and every meeting could become 'see the result, then react.' Rate surprises transmit through debt and leverage to all assets, so volatility needs repricing. The hosts also assert from history: once truly tested by markets, nearly every official eventually caves, so the current promise of 'never pre-empting market expectations' is itself the variable most worth testing.

17:31 Midterm election volatility is priced like an ordinary day
Kevin Muir argues that midterm election volatility is severely underpriced. During the 2022 midterms, options priced a ±1.8% one-day move in the S&P on voting day; in 2018 it was ±1.25%; now it's only ±0.9%. And this time Trump's approval is at historic lows, and he just spent a prime-time hour talking about 'election fraud,' as if laying groundwork to challenge the result. Muir notes: even if you think he's overreacting, that's fine—as voting day nears, the question of 'will the election be contested' will itself be repriced. With volatility near seasonal lows and implied correlation at historic lows, the odds for long volatility are much better than usual.

23:41 Disinflation is a supply illusion; demand hasn't cooled
Ahan Manon splits PCE components into 'demand-driven' and 'supply-driven.' Their contributions are now 3.31 vs. 0.38; even if you completely strip out the energy supply shock from Iran, the remaining demand side alone is enough to keep inflation above the Fed's 2% target. Historically, demand-driven inflation is slow and persistent, while supply-driven inflation tends to spike quickly and mean-revert within 6 to 12 months. The breadth is more troubling: in recent months, 70% to 80% of PCE components are rising faster than 2%. June saw a negative month-over-month print and July only rebounded 16 basis points, but these short-term cooling effects are almost entirely from the supply side; the demand-driven trend hasn't been interrupted.

34:51 One hike could have fixed credibility; he didn't do it
Ben Hunt says Warsh hit a 'self-goal' at the post-July-FOMC press conference. Earlier, the new face and hawkish inflation rhetoric had largely repaired the 'Fed credibility' narrative; but the real move was to hike 25 basis points immediately. Just that one hike would convince markets that 'he means what he says,' and no repeated hikes would be needed. Skipping that step reversed the narrative completely: every independent report in the financial press that week said the same thing in different words—'meet the new boss, same as the old boss.' Credibility, once broken, is hard to glue back; August's gold rally is the market's reaction to 'hawkish talk, no action.'

40:13 After the credibility wound, only jawboning financial repression remains
Ben Hunt lists four pressures the Fed and Treasury must manage but cannot let blow up: the Iran war has no easy exit and oil stays higher for longer; fiscal stimulus fades and tariff pressures return; the insurance sector has a systemic problem with captive insurers being used to take on private investments; and the 10- and 30-year long-end rates cannot be allowed to rise. Any one could be the fuse for the next financial crisis. Handling these requires credibility, which was just wounded, so all policy choices are reduced to 'jawboning financial repression'—using statements and intervention to cap yields rather than letting markets price them. His judgment: this operation has no maturity date; it only accelerates.

49:25 Options market treats Fed meetings like any other day
Brent Kachuba shows an options term structure with almost no event risk: the 0DTE straddle on the day of Warsh's speech is worth only 38 index points; SPX options expiring August 31 have implied volatility of just 7%, the overall term structure is at 90-day lows, and put open interest is low. He usually avoids trading Fed events because events turn options into a 'tax'—premium is collected before the event, and time value decays once it passes. But this time is special because the market has compressed volatility expectations to near zero and no one is hedging; before Jackson Hole he bought some 'lottery tickets' with very cheap short-dated put spreads, because if Warsh says one thing the market doesn't like, naked option sellers will get squeezed instantly. After the event passes, that's a better time to follow directional trends.

58:42 Outsourcing writing to AI outsources thinking too
The closing topic is Druckenmiller's WSJ op-ed: he publicly said it was written by AI, with the simple reason that AI writes better than he does. The hosts argue the key is whether the views and emotions belong to the author; Druckenmiller's piece reads like his usual gut judgments, with AI only organizing and expressing, so it's not deception. Ben Hunt draws the line at writing itself: writing is part of the thinking process—'I write to figure out what I think.' When the text-generation step is outsourced, readers lose an important clue: whether the author actually thought through these words. Obvious AI products are already flooding investment blogs; to judge whether an opinion is reliable, don't just look at how polished the prose is—ask whether the view has a thinking process behind it.

item.description: China's share of global GDP peaked in 2021 and has been declining since; credit growth has fallen from 18% to 5%, and real growth may be only 1.5%-2%; the US has outperformed for five consecutive years. The narrative of industrial chain dominance is disproven by data; the future looks more like Japan-style deflation.
item.content:encoded:
China's share of global GDP peaked in 2021 and has been declining since; credit growth has fallen from 18% to 5%, and real growth may be only 1.5%-2%; the US has outperformed for five consecutive years. The narrative of industrial chain dominance is disproven by data; the future looks more like Japan-style deflation.

To counter the mainstream narrative that 'China's new industries = growth engine,' grounding judgments in verifiable data on credit, special bonds, and demographics; for those who want to update their long-term view of China and the US.

0:05 China has missed its window to overtake the US
Dmitri sets the tone with official data: China's share of global GDP peaked at 18.5% in 2021 and has declined each year since; the US has risen from 24% to about 26%. He concludes that China has almost no chance of replacing the US as the world's largest economy, and the US economic advantage may widen further over the next decade. Logan fully agrees and steers the discussion toward a 'decline, not collapse' framework.

2:11 The root of China's slowdown is the end of credit expansion
Logan attributes China's slowdown to the end of extraordinary credit expansion. After the financial crisis, China added credit equivalent to one-third of global GDP in eight years; credit growth fell from an average of 18% in 2007-2016 to 9% after 2017, and now stands at just over 5%. Once credit stops, borrowers cannot refinance and investment slows. Official figures still report 5.2% growth in 2023 and 5% in 2024 and 2025, but he estimates real growth since 2022 has been only 1.5%-2%, already below the US.

6:14 Using purchasing power parity rewards deflation
Addressing the common rebuttal that 'China has already surpassed the US in PPP terms,' Logan says PPP comparisons are still meaningful for developing countries but untenable between the world's two largest economies: scoring by PPP rewards China for producing deflation—the lower domestic prices are, the stronger the economy appears, yet deflation is precisely the problem. He also stresses that debt is repaid in nominal local currency, so nominal GDP matters; the exchange rate is not an exogenous variable but an external signal of China's policy capacity.

13:25 Capital controls are not a cure, only a time-buyer
Logan concedes that China's capital controls are effective but argues they are not a panacea for massive macroeconomic imbalances. The impossible trinity dictates that free capital flow, exchange rate stability, and monetary policy independence can only be achieved two at a time. The function of capital controls is to delay outflows, suppress rapid cross-border volatility, and channel outflows into government-visible avenues—Huawei and BYD can go global aggressively, while private firms like HNA had their overseas acquisitions halted in 2016; this is the two sides of the screening mechanism.

17:35 Credit still subsidizes old industries, not new ones
Logan rebuts the claim that 'credit is shifting to more productive new industries': central bank data show that the share of loans issued at or below the Loan Prime Rate has risen from the 20s to 59%, indicating banks are continuously subsidizing. The share of special revenue bonds directed to so-called strategic industries rose only from about 2% in 2021 to 6% in 2025, with the vast majority still going to traditional sectors. Using the 2023 input-output table, he estimates that electric vehicles, batteries, AI, and solar together account for about 6.3% of GDP, while the decline in real estate and infrastructure investment is about six times the increase from these new industries.

27:45 Europe is the last buyer of China's excess capacity
Logan judges that if Europe turns protectionist, China will be 'truly finished': the US market has narrowed and transshipment space is limited, and the developing world cannot absorb China's excess capacity while maintaining its own growth. He warns that the US focus on bilateral trade deficits is wrong—deficits are determined by the savings-investment gap; tariffs only redistribute deficits, and not addressing the fundamental imbalance will only breed more transshipment trade.

34:58 Without touching taxes, domestic demand won't take off
Logan draws a parallel with Soviet Kosygin reforms: Brezhnev chose to pivot to a technological revolution rather than push reforms and maintain ideology. To convert savings into consumption, the real lever is tax policy—extracting resources from high-net-worth individuals, state-owned enterprises, and private firms excluded from the financial system. But he thinks it is almost unimaginable that Xi Jinping would go on TV to announce that 'the fiscal and financial system of the past 15 years will no longer apply in the future'; Beijing's insistence on the 5% growth narrative is partly to undermine export controls and discourage Western investment in alternative supply chains.

39:00 China in 2035 will look like Japan today
Logan predicts that without major policy changes, China's economy in 2035 will resemble Japan's: persistent deflation, persistent external surpluses, exchange rate depreciation pressure, and low interest rates. The hardest constraint is demographics—China's actual average age at death is 73, and the early PRC baby boom will bring a population decline of 50-60 million over the next decade, about 3%-4% of the total population; even maintaining last year's low birth rate of 7.92 million won't stop it. He also notes that the fiscal deficit is already close to $2 trillion per year, about 9.5% of GDP, leaving fewer resources available than in the past. He concludes that if China truly wins by export share, it will invite stronger political backlash—'winning is losing.'

item.title: Bell Used Einstein's Own Tools to Refute His Core Argument
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-theoriesofever-贝尔用爱因斯坦自己的工具推翻了他的核心论点/

item.description: The EPR argument forces a choice between an incomplete quantum description and action at a distance; determinism is never an assumption but a conclusion that is inferred. The full logic of Bell's theorem must start here.
item.content:encoded:
The EPR argument forces a choice between an incomplete quantum description and action at a distance; determinism is never an assumption but a conclusion that is inferred. The full logic of Bell's theorem must start here.

Maudlin walks from the 1905 photoelectric effect to the 1964 Bell inequality, breaking the EPR argument into steps that can be checked one by one. For those who want to truly understand nonlocality rather than memorize conclusions.

3:05 The father of quantum theory is Einstein, not Planck
Although Planck is usually regarded as the father of quantum theory, it was Einstein's 1905 paper on the photoelectric effect that actually proposed the quantization hypothesis. Planck only did statistical calculations, while Einstein explicitly argued that energy is transferred in discrete quanta. Maudlin deliberately corrects this historical attribution.

45:32 A single particle is enough to force action at a distance
Einstein's objection at the 1927 Solvay Conference was: if the wave function completely describes a single particle, and the wave spreads in all directions toward the screen, then the particle could produce effects at multiple locations simultaneously. To avoid multiple-point effects, one must introduce an instantaneous and global collapse mechanism of the wave function—this is action at a distance. Note, this is not about superluminal signaling.

1:14:50 If the wave function is real, locality has no place to reside
The wave function of a many-particle system is defined on configuration space, not physical space; for example, a two-particle system is a six-dimensional configuration space. In classical mechanics, configuration space is a mathematical convenience, but if the wave function is treated as fundamental reality, configuration space becomes the physical stage, and the definition of local forces in each small spatial region becomes problematic. This is another layer of Einstein's concern about dynamical locality.

1:31:59 EPR's reality criterion cannot be coherently denied
EPR's reality criterion says: if, without disturbing a system, one can predict with probability 1 the value of a physical quantity, then that quantity corresponds to an element of physical reality. Maudlin emphasizes that this is a sufficient condition, not a necessary one. He refutes common attempts to deny the criterion, arguing that it is analytic and cannot be coherently denied. This sets the stage for the subsequent either-or conclusion.

2:02:26 Either the description is incomplete, or accept action at a distance
Because the reality criterion cannot be denied, the EPR argument forces a dilemma: either accept that the quantum description is incomplete, or accept that Alice's operation in her lab indeed disturbs the physical state of Bob's particle—that is, action at a distance. Einstein found action at a distance absurd and therefore chose incompleteness. This is the logical exit of the entire EPR argument.

2:10:34 Denying determinism does not escape Bell's conclusion
Maudlin repeatedly emphasizes that in the EPR argument determinism is not assumed but inferred from perfect correlations and locality. He quotes Bell's own words: 'Insofar as determinism plays a role in the EPR argument, it is not assumed but inferred.' Therefore, attempts to escape Bell's conclusion by denying determinism are completely ineffective.

2:43:53 Bohr's famous response was understood by no one
Faced with the EPR argument, Bohr had only two logically possible responses: accept action at a distance, or admit that the quantum description is incomplete. But Bohr chose neither. Maudlin says his response paper is 'a mess' that no one can understand. He even mentions that in the book edited by Wheeler and Zurek, two pages of Bohr's article are reversed in order, yet no one noticed because no one could follow the logic anyway.

2:55:02 Any local theory gives wrong predictions
Bell's starting point was precisely the EPR paper, yet his conclusion was that Einstein's fundamental claim about 'no action at a distance' was wrong: any local theory fails to make correct predictions. Maudlin calls this a great ironic reversal—Bell used Einstein's own tools to refute his fundamental argument. This is the true entry point for understanding why Bell's theorem matters.

item.title: The Quantum Endgame Isn't Cleaner Qubits — It's Who Can Use a Phone-Chip Fab Line
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-fromfirstprinc-硅自旋将赢-百万比特只需一块硅晶圆/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-fromfirstprinc-硅自旋将赢-百万比特只需一块硅晶圆/
item.description: The quantum endgame isn't about who has cleaner qubits — it's about who can mass-produce using existing semiconductor fabs. Silicon spin qubits reuse TSMC lithography, while ion traps are stuck at a hundred thousand laser beams and superconductors at warehouse-sized refrigerators.
item.content:encoded:
The quantum endgame isn't about who has cleaner qubits — it's about who can mass-produce using existing semiconductor fabs. Silicon spin qubits reuse TSMC lithography, while ion traps are stuck at a hundred thousand laser beams and superconductors at warehouse-sized refrigerators.

The exclusive value is in the second half: HRL paper's CNOT error rate, AI auto-tuning, and FFP's striking scores. The first half's principle explanations are more introductory; veterans can fast-forward.

0:00 Ion traps and superconductors need miracles first; silicon doesn't
To build a 100,000-qubit ion trap, you'd first have to invent the optical miracle of 100,000 laser beams; for a million superconducting qubits, you'd need a cryostat the size of a warehouse; a million spin qubits only require a standard 300mm silicon wafer, run through the same lithography equipment TSMC, ASML, and Intel use to make phone processors. Krishna uses this to set the tone for the whole episode: the key to the quantum race isn't single-qubit fidelity, but whether the scaling path already exists in the industrial system.

32:48 Quantum computing is no longer about principles, but engineering
In 2000, DiVincenzo proposed five criteria, aiming to dismiss liquid-state NMR quantum computing. This episode of FFP proposes its own three criteria: qubit quality, control, and scalability with economics. The rest of the episode scores four routes — superconducting, ion trap, neutral atom, and silicon spin — item by item. Laying out the evaluation system itself tells you: quantum computing has entered the stage of engineering competition; you can't just talk about principles.

1:24:33 Superconducting isn't a technical failure, it's an engineering impossibility
Estimates show that a thousand logical qubits would require ten million transmon physical qubits. Control line count is limited by the cooling capacity of dilution refrigerators, frequency crowding occurs, and helium-3 supply becomes a new resource constraint. FFP gives superconducting only 1/10 on scalability and economics, with a total score of 11/30. This is the first time the show separates 'technically strong' from 'engineering infeasible' — a warehouse-sized refrigerator means even data centers might not fit it.

1:47:08 Ion traps win on coherence time, lose on gate speed
Ion trap coherence times reach ten hours, but gate operations rely on phonons, limited by the Paul trap oscillation frequency, making them about a thousand times slower than superconducting. The result is counterintuitive: even if ion traps could scale to break encryption, cracking 2048-bit RSA would take about a year, while superconducting would take only about eight hours. Long coherence time doesn't mean more work per unit time; for practical computation, slow gate time is a throughput disaster overall.

2:03:32 The quantum threat is neither tomorrow nor never
A March 2026 paper from Harvard, Caltech, and Qera says 10,000 qubits might break internet encryption, but it would actually take several years; even with 100,000 physical qubits, under mathematically optimal assumptions, breaking RSA would take about three months. This number strikes both extreme narratives: the quantum threat is not tomorrow, but it is certainly not forever distant. To achieve 'breakable within months' requires qubit count, gate speed, and error correction all to meet standards simultaneously.

2:50:02 Quantum companies live or die by government contracts
HRL lost key project funding in early 2026 and laid off 376 people. Government funding shifted from basic research to applied research demanding rapid commercialization; IBM and Intel received support from the CHIPS Act, and ultimately IBM acquired HRL. Krishna calls this the debut of quantum computing's MVP: quantum companies' fates depend on government contracts, and being acquired isn't failure — it's getting the technology into an industrial system with manufacturing capability.

3:23:10 A million qubits can't be tuned by hand — only by image recognition
Automated tuning becomes key to scaling: a 2023 paper could tune six electrons by hand, but manual tuning of a million qubits would take a human lifetime. Tuning is essentially image recognition — when scanning voltage, tunneling events appear as stripes. Krishna's team uses DETR, combining ResNet and Transformer, to automatically recognize stripes and generate parameters. This is also the hidden premise for why silicon spin can reuse semiconductor fabs: no matter how many qubits, software can align them automatically.

3:32:31 Silicon may not be first, but it will be last to win
FFP's final scores: silicon spin gets 10/10 on qubit quality, 10/10 on control (provided isotope enrichment and valley state issues are solved), and 10000/10 on scalability and economics, for a total of 10020/30; neutral atoms score negative 3000. Krishna admits silicon may not be the first route to achieve fault tolerance, but once it does, it will become the final standard because it's cheap and manufacturable, just as transistors replaced vacuum tubes.

item.title: AI Chip Shipments Will Jump an Order of Magnitude: From a Million to 15 Million
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-techtechpotato-未来-ai-定制芯片的形态-一只带-16-个-hbm-的巨兽/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-techtechpotato-未来-ai-定制芯片的形态-一只带-16-个-hbm-的巨兽/
item.description: Broadcom's president shows an AI chip roadmap: from a million units to 15 million, with the 'beast' being the largest package of 8 stackable compute dies plus 16 HBM modules, and four of the five frontier labs are collaborating.
item.content:encoded:
Broadcom's president shows an AI chip roadmap: from a million units to 15 million, with the 'beast' being the largest package of 8 stackable compute dies plus 16 HBM modules, and four of the five frontier labs are collaborating.

Broadcom rarely discloses details, but this time it gave three package tiers and three shipment volumes, plus a clear judgment on the HBM bottleneck. For those tracking ASIC and packaging, these 11 minutes are more informative than many long analyses.

1:06 Custom chip makers still outsource the final step
Google, Meta, Amazon, and some frontier model companies can have their own chip design teams, define their own architecture and interconnect, but ultimately they still have to 'get the thing built': dealing with foundries and development kits, managing the timing and latency of connections between transistors. Broadcom is the largest of these fee-based back-end design service providers. Clients come to it not just for design capability, but also for a batch of ready-made IP including high-speed I/O, high-speed compute, and memory controllers.

3:09 The most tight-lipped chip company suddenly starts talking
Broadcom is a mystery externally: it has almost no PR department and rarely discloses proactively. Occasionally it releases a Tomahawk network chip, or chats with Patrick Kennedy on ServeTheHome. Over the past year, president Charlie has rarely taken the stage at launch events to talk about what Broadcom is doing and why it is expanding its customer base from traditional network chips to custom AI chips. The chart showing three tiers of chips is the clue.

4:09 Today's AI servers are just the smallest of three tiers
Of the three tiers Charlie showed, the leftmost is already shipping in hundreds of thousands of systems, about the size of this Cisco chip on the desk: one compute die in the middle, surrounded by four to six HBM modules, packaged with something like TSMC's CoWoS. Broadcom says that over the past year, it has shipped more than one million units of this tier for customers. This tier is the reality of today's AI servers.

5:09 The larger the package, the higher the shipment volume
The middle tier is noticeably larger: two to four compute/IO dies, surrounded by eight to twelve HBM modules; AMD's MI455X also fits this design form. Charlie's expected shipment volumes are key: the middle tier is expected to ship 5 million units, and the rightmost tier 15 million. Placed next to 'one million units over the past year,' this is not linear growth but an order-of-magnitude jump in shipments for the next generation of custom AI chips.

6:11 The rightmost chip may stack compute dies on compute dies
The rightmost 'beast': the red parts are eight compute dies arranged in two columns of four, and they are stacked. Charlie lifts the red to reveal purple underneath, which could be SRAM, or SRAM could be on top; if it is compute-on-compute, it effectively equals sixteen compute dies. Each compute die is paired with two HBM modules, so one package contains sixteen HBM modules, with two light-blue IO dies at the top and bottom edges, and openings left at the package edges for optical modules.

7:11 Almost all frontier model companies are making their own chips
Charlie said that of the five most advanced frontier model labs, four are working with Broadcom on custom compute chips. Companies like OpenAI and Anthropic define the designs they want, Broadcom does the back-end services and interfaces with TSMC, and then partners like Supermicro and WiWynn are brought in for data center scale deployment. This also explains why Broadcom is expanding capacity: it not only serves traditional network customers but is also taking orders from large model companies.

9:11 The bottleneck to scaling may not be packaging but HBM
The real bottleneck may not be packaging but whether there is enough high-bandwidth memory to go around: could a new form between DDR/LPDDR and HBM emerge to fill the gap? Additionally, Broadcom said on stage that it has already deployed a 2nm chip with a partner, slightly smaller than the beast and closer in time. This reminds us that in the coming years, advanced packaging and HBM capacity will be swept up along with custom chip orders.

10:13 The first 2nm custom chip to land may come from Japan
The host pinned down the 'coming soon, smaller' 2nm chip Broadcom mentioned: he asked George from Chips and Cheese, and the two judged it to be Fujitsu's Monaka—a 2nm compute die paired with a 5nm SRAM die, with a central IO die in between. This chip has previously appeared as a mockup or test silicon at several conferences.

item.title: An Explorer Died for a Fictional City, and It All Started with a Political Forgery
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-stuffmissed-福西特不是去冒险-是去给橡胶资本画地图/

item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: Percy Fawcett's Amazon expeditions are often told as adventure legends, but the real starting point was border disputes fueled by the rubber trade; his narrative of 'respect' for indigenous people is a gross oversimplification, and the City of Z that obsessed him may rest on a forged manuscript.
item.content:encoded:
Percy Fawcett's Amazon expeditions are often told as adventure legends, but the real starting point was border disputes fueled by the rubber trade; his narrative of 'respect' for indigenous people is a gross oversimplification, and the City of Z that obsessed him may rest on a forged manuscript.

This episode has medium information density, but it clearly lays out the beginnings of the rubber trade, indigenous catastrophe, and Manuscript 512; listeners only seeking adventure anecdotes may find the first half's setup a bit long.

3:04 His obsession began with a Roman well in childhood
Fawcett was born in 1867. His family was nominally aristocratic, but his father, Edward Fawcett, had squandered the fortune and could only serve as a private assistant to Queen Victoria's son 'Bertie' (later Edward VII). Fawcett described a childhood in Torquay lacking parental affection, which made him introverted. His sister recalled that as a child he discovered a well full of Roman pottery on Halden Moors, and had his siblings lower him down to retrieve the artifacts and take them to a museum. This boldness, stubbornness, and outward-seeking personality later reappeared in his fixation on the occult and the Amazon.

8:13 An officer who held séances still rose to major
In 1901 Fawcett married Nina, and in 1903 their first son Jack was born. That same year he was posted to Spike Island off the south coast of Ireland. Fawcett found the posting dull, so he spent his spare time conducting séances. His interest in the occult was not a fringe hobby; his son Brian later wrote that anyone who sought knowledge beyond the material might be called a mystic. This interest did not hinder his military career—he was promoted to major. This shows that Fawcett's 'rationality' and 'superstition' coexisted, setting the stage for his later credulity toward Manuscript 512.

10:19 His first Amazon trip was a diplomatic mission, not an adventure
In 1901 Fawcett joined the Royal Geographical Society and completed specialized training in boundary demarcation. In 1906 the Society's president, Sir George Goldie, met with him and asked about his knowledge of Bolivia, then told him: border disputes among Brazil, Peru, and Bolivia had escalated because of the rubber trade, and the countries involved would not accept demarcation by any interested party, so the Bolivian government asked the Royal Geographical Society to arbitrate and recommend an officer. For Fawcett, this was a chance to 'escape the monotony of an artillery officer's life'; he was 39, and his wife was pregnant with their second child. The chain of argument here is: rubber's economic value → territorial disputes → Britain as a 'disinterested' third party → Fawcett enters the Amazon as a surveyor. The counterintuitive point is that his initial expedition was not self-directed adventure but commercial and diplomatic arrangement.

14:25 He was attacked everywhere because 90% of natives were already dead
Before he reached South America, the rubber industry had already transformed the region. Figures cited in the episode: before Europeans arrived, the area of present-day Brazil had at least 2,000 indigenous tribes with a total population of about 11 million; in the first hundred years after colonists arrived in the 16th century, 90% of indigenous people died from disease or genocide, and survivors were often enslaved for rubber work. The rubber trade made land extremely valuable, and Europeans moved in and seized indigenous lands, leading natives to view all Europeans as threats—this is the backdrop for Fawcett's hostile encounters. His own accounts also show he was well aware of European colonial atrocities. This section provides a structural explanation for 'why he was attacked everywhere' and corrects the romanticized narrative of 'explorer in peril.'

17:28 Calling him respectful of natives sets the bar too low
Fawcett's dealings with indigenous people were not solely confrontational. He would insist that he and his companions lay down their arms and show they posed no threat; he also learned local languages and condemned the earlier European colonists for creating the problems that continued to sour relations. But at the same time, much of what he wrote was 'extremely racist' and condescending. The hosts state plainly that later accounts often describe him as 'respectful of indigenous people,' which is an oversimplification; even if he was 'often better' than contemporary European explorers, that bar is shockingly low. The value here: many popular narratives today cast Fawcett as an enlightened explorer, and the episode dismantles that myth with specific written evidence, without reducing his behavior to that of a pure villain.

19:28 He survived an ambush with an accordion, not a gun
This is one of Fawcett's most famous escape stories. His expedition was ambushed on a river by indigenous archers, and peaceful calls went unanswered. He had his companion Todd sit on a log mid-river with an accordion and start playing, while the others sang loudly and stomped their feet. Before long, the hail of arrows stopped, and a wide-eyed native peered out from the bushes; the expedition was then welcomed into the village and even given help. This example shows Fawcett was not solely violent; his tools for problem-solving included music and clownish performance. It also shows that his records contain both observations worth taking seriously and plenty of unreliable exaggeration, setting up contrasts with later descriptions of giant anacondas, peanuts, and double-nosed dogs.

25:32 He believed in a lost city because old documents really mentioned one
Before World War I, Fawcett efficiently completed map surveys (often much faster than expected) while becoming increasingly fascinated by claims of lost cities in the jungle. He named the city he sought 'Zed' and located it in Mato Grosso, a non-coastal state in southern Brazil; it covers about 900,000 square kilometers, is densely forested, and remains one of Brazil's least densely populated regions even today. In the early 20th century, almost no Europeans had entered it. The chain of argument: numerous 16th- and 17th-century Spanish and Portuguese explorer documents described 'very advanced large cities' → Fawcett believed they were real → he grew increasingly obsessed with finding the City of Z.

29:40 The manuscript he believed without reservation may be a hoax
After the war, Fawcett continued studying old documents, most often citing Manuscript 512, held in the National Library of Rio de Janeiro: a Portuguese adventurer's 1753 account of his experiences in the Amazon, sometimes attributed to João de Silvestre de Moraes. Fawcett gave the author the pseudonym Francisco Raposo and wrote that he believed the manuscript's contents 'without reservation,' calling it an 'incomparable story.' However, at the start of the episode, the hosts had already warned that this document 'is likely a hoax.' So the real suspense is not whether the lost city existed, but why a trained geography officer would be so captivated by a possibly forged 1753 record.

item.title: Time Is Not an Illusion: Irreversibility Is More Fundamental Than Symmetric Equations
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-mindscape-时间的方向性比时间对称方程更根本/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-08-31-mindscape-时间的方向性比时间对称方程更根本/
item.description: Jim Al-Khalili argues that time is real and directed, and that irreversibility is more fundamental than time-symmetric equations; he also proposes using quantum entanglement entropy instead of thermodynamic entropy as the basis for the past hypothesis.
item.content:encoded:
Jim Al-Khalili argues that time is real and directed, and that irreversibility is more fundamental than time-symmetric equations; he also proposes using quantum entanglement entropy instead of thermodynamic entropy as the basis for the past hypothesis.

Sean Carroll and Jim Al-Khalili hold opposing views on the arrow of time, and this episode reveals their real points of divergence; the latter half also covers quantum biology mechanisms and a new hypothesis about quantum entanglement entropy.

4:07 Time's direction is built in, not emergent
Jim takes a hard stance: time is real and tangible, part of four-dimensional spacetime, not just something clocks measure. He goes further, saying that time's directionality is not emergent from directionless fundamental laws but is built into the universe. Sean reminds listeners that this is a big controversy—many physicists think time is just a tool or that direction is a product of coarse-graining. Jim's intuition is that, viewed from inside the universe, irreversibility is the more fundamental thing.

17:38 No system is isolated, so irreversibility is the norm
The traditional narrative is that fundamental equations like Newton's and Schrödinger's are invariant under time reversal, and the arrow of time must emerge from entropy increase or coarse-graining. Jim turns this around: time-symmetric equations are idealizations because no system is truly isolated—even quantum systems are constantly entangled with their environment. Time-symmetric equations apply only to isolated systems and are a special case of the master equation; in reality, everything exchanges energy and information with its environment, and irreversibility is the norm. He admits this is a minority view but believes it is closer to the real world.

27:50 The special moment must be at the Big Bang, not last week
If you treat the entire universe as an isolated system that also obeys time-symmetric laws, then by the second law, yesterday's entropy should be higher than today's, not lower. The only way out is to push that special moment to the very beginning: the Big Bang. That is the past hypothesis. Jim stresses that this is not an extra assumption but part of the universe's initial conditions, alongside fine-tuning of constants. He agrees with Sean: if you must pick a special moment, the Big Bang is far more reasonable than last week.

31:03 Physical laws contain no flow of time, yet we feel it
Even if low-entropy initial conditions explain the arrow of time, Sean presses: where do psychological experiences like 'now' and the sense of passage come from? Jim honestly admits that physical laws contain no flow of time, yet we feel time flowing. He says this is a gap between physical time and manifest time, and he is not even sure how to articulate it clearly. This candor is more valuable than pretending to have solved it, and it shows the problem of time is far from closed.

45:51 DNA mutations may come from a proton's quantum tunneling
From a nuclear physicist's perspective, Jim presents the most concrete case in quantum biology: DNA's double helix is held together by hydrogen bonds, and the hydrogen atom is essentially a proton. Löwdin proposed in the early 1960s that a proton could quantum-tunnel through the energy barrier to the opposite strand, causing a mutation during replication. Jim's team has done increasingly refined calculations to determine the ratio of tunneling to thermal excitation. He points out that quantum biology is not the old saw that 'atoms are quantum' but asks whether life has evolved to exploit long-lived coherence and entanglement.

1:03:12 A more fundamental version of the past hypothesis is entanglement entropy
The thermodynamic past hypothesis requires specifying a low-entropy microstate. Jim and philosopher Eddy Chen have attempted a more quantum version: assume the universe began in a pure state with extremely low entanglement entropy, with subsystems barely entangled. As it evolves, subsystems become increasingly entangled, and the universe's total entanglement entropy rises monotonically. Conceptually this is more fundamental than thermodynamic entropy, but Jim admits there are many gaps—for instance, how finely to partition subsystems. This direction is still unfinished.

1:12:29 After cosmic heat death, time still passes
Many say time might disappear at extreme scales. Jim counters: even tens of trillions of years from now, when the universe reaches thermal equilibrium and no change can be used to measure time, time still passes. He admits this is not time in the relativistic sense that holds in every reference frame, but it makes time almost return to Newton's absolute clock—a real occurrence. For him, even if time emerges from something more fundamental, that does not mean it is not real.
